articles.content:
At the 2026 League of Legends World Championship Finals, Riot Games officially unveiled League of Legends: New Dawn. The large-scale update is scheduled for 2027 and will bring changes to the game's client, Summoner's Rift, visuals, and gameplay, marking the beginning of a new chapter for one of the industry's most enduring titles.

New Dawn introduces what Riot described as an "all-encompassing" update to League, touching almost every aspect of its experience. "This is the start of a new era for League, a new journey," said Paul Bellezza, League's executive producer, in New Dawn's first official trailer. Riot is expected to share the full reveal of New Dawn this coming January.

A peek at where we’re headed for 2027 https://t.co/Wqem6t48pn

— League of Legends @ Worlds 2026 (@LeagueOfLegends) November 14, 2026

A new look for Summoner's Rift

The announcement came with a trailer shown at Worlds Finals that offered the first glimpse of what League players can expect from New Dawn, and the changes appear to go beyond simple refreshed graphics. The first noticeable change is a redesigned champion selection screen, which looks much closer to the modern interface found in Wild Rift, League's mobile game. The footage also hints at a new or reworked rune system, which seems to have a much bigger impact on the gameplay than ever before.

The trailer also showcased updated minions, a new look for Summoner's Rift, redesigned dragons and Baron Nashor, as well as what seem to be new visual effects for many champion abilities. More interestingly, the footage also hinted at gameplay changes that will change how players approach their matches, including major changes to the map terrain that open new strategic consideration — and not only for junglers.

Since its launch in 2009, League has seen more than a few major changes, including a rebuilt Summoner's Rift in 2014, a new client a couple of years later, and runes and then terrain changes in the following years. Still, nothing ever came close to the scale of what New Dawn promises to be. For now, Riot is keeping the full extent of these gameplay changes to itself, leaving much of New Dawn's scope to be revealed in the coming months.

Leaving the past behind

Riot spent part of 2026 looking back at League's history through League Classic, a mode that allowed players to revisit older versions of both the Summoner's Rift and League's champions. However, nostalgia alone proved difficult to sustain. Just a few weeks after its release, Riot announced that the mode would end its current run in January 2027. The experience could return in a modified format in the future, but it demonstrated that revisiting the past is not necessarily enough to keep a game of League's scale moving forward.

Now, Riot is looking in the opposite direction. 18 years since League first launched, New Dawn represents another attempt at evolving a game whose identity has been shaped as much by its community as by its developers. But whether players embrace the changes or push back against them remains to be seen. After all, it is the playerbase that will ultimately decide whether this new chapter gives League the foundation it needs to thrive for another decade or sends it down a different path.

More information about League of Legends: New Dawn is expected in the coming weeks, with Riot's full presentation scheduled for some time in January 2027.

articles.title: Resident Evil Requiem Star Hopes Grace Ashcroft Has 'a Long Way to Go' Even if She Won't 'Ever Be a Leon Character'
articles.description: Grace Ashcroft actress Angela Sant'Albano doesn't think her Resident Evil Requiem hero will "ever be a Leon character," but she's still hoping "there's a long way to go with her."
articles.content:
Grace Ashcroft actress Angela Sant'Albano doesn't think her Resident Evil Requiem hero will "ever be a Leon character," but she's still hoping "there's a long way to go with her."

The person behind one of 2026's standout video game roles laid out her hopes for the future during an interview with GamesRadar. Resident Evil Requiem may only be a few months old, but she's already got a good idea of how she'd like to see Grace grow should she be asked to brave manmade horrors beyond comprehension yet again.

Warning! Spoilers for Resident Evil Requiem follow.

"I would really love to see how her relationship with Leon blossoms," Sant'Albano explained. "I think we have a beautiful mentorship, almost brotherly, sisterly relationship brewing. And I also want to know what happens with her and Emily."

Assuming you chose the 'good' ending, Resident Evil Requiem closes with the series' one-liner expert, Leon S. Kennedy, alive and Grace taking Emily under her wing. It painted a bright future for the crew, and although it almost certainly won't last, it did give the developers at Capcom plenty of room to grow new and old characters alike.

Despite some pretty deep roots in Resident Evil lore, Grace's story in the franchise is really only getting started in Resident Evil Requiem. So far, there's been no word on whether she'll stick around for additional entries and eventually stand toe-to-toe with other protagonists like Ethan Winters or Chris Redfield. Judging by the strong impression she made when her debut game launched in February, we wouldn't be surprised to see her back at some point down the line.

Sant'Albano knows Grace could survive another run in with mutated monsters after making it through the horrors of the Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Center, but will she ever be dodging chainsaws with carefully timed but stylish backflips? Not likely.

"I don't think she'll ever be a Leon character," Sant'Albano said. "She's never going to be badass, you know, doing roundhouse kicks. But I do think her courage and her self-esteem will grow the more that she trusts herself and forgives herself for a lot of the things that I think tie her down. So, I think there's a long way to go with her."

Resident Evil Requiem is still so fresh, so we probably won't hear about another mainline entry like a potential Resident Evil 10 anytime soon. As if there was any doubt, that doesn't mean Capcom plans to keep players waiting for more.

In 2027, fans will step back into the shoes of Resident Evil 2 hero Claire Redfield for Resident Evil Veronica. It's been a while since we last heard an update on that front following its announcement in June. We're also still waiting to hear more about the story DLC the publisher promised back in March. Maybe we could see more Grace there?

IGN gave Resident Evil Requiem a 9/10 review. At the time of its launch, we said it "successfully splices two separate strains of survival horror together into one highly infectious new mutation."

articles.title: 'It Felt Criminal' — Adam Driver Still Can't Believe How Disney Handled Canceled Star Wars Movie The Hunt for Ben Solo
articles.description: Adam Driver still can't believe Disney killed his Star Wars movie, The Hunt for Ben Solo, and has now gone so far as to say that the move "felt criminal."
articles.content:
Adam Driver still can't believe Disney killed his Star Wars movie, The Hunt for Ben Solo, and has now gone so far as to say that the move "felt criminal."

The Kylo Ren/Ben Solo actor relived some of the darker parts of his past with the massive sci-fi franchise during a recent conversation with AP. His updated thoughts on the matter follow years of work and months of fan organizing, and although he and director Steven Soderbergh have almost nothing to show for it, he's still pretty fired up about how it all went down.

"For me it was: Steven Soderbergh wants to make a Star Wars film," Driver said. "What are we debating? It’s what it is. It’s criminal. Or it felt criminal. We’re all moving on. On to the next. And Steven already has something else that’s one of the best things he’s ever written."

We first learned about The Hunt for Ben Solo, a Skywalker Saga follow-up that explored a potential future for its title character, when Driver called it one of the "coolest scripts" he had "ever been a part of" late last year. Despite the hype, it never came to be, mostly because, according to Driver, then-Disney CEO Bob Iger and co-chairman Alan Bergman "didn't see how Ben Solo was alive."

What followed was months of additional words from those who worked on the shuttered project, including Soderbergh, who called Disney's decision to pull the plug after two-and-a-half years of work "insane." Before long, fans orchestrated their own campaign to try and save the movie, but at least as far as August 2026, Lucasfilm president Dave Filoni has said that it's not something the company is working on right now.

With so much work put into it, it's been hard for many to see why Disney would shut down an impassioned pitch from a fan-favorite Star Wars actor. Driver himself still seems confused about the call to this day. The silver lining, though, was how dedicated fans chipped in to see his and Soderbergh's ideas brought to life.

"I was blown away by the response to it," Driver added. "In no way did I think there would be billboards in Times Square. It’s so moving. It did feel like we were all at the bar having a conversation about the films we wanted to see."

For now, however, Driver is most likely hanging up his hilted lightsaber for good. He said as much during another interview earlier this month, though he's still leaving the door open should Disney change its mind about The Hunt for Ben Solo. Soderbergh, who is currently helping out with The Batman Part 2, ruled out a return in April of this year.

Taika Waititi's long-gestating Star Wars movie joined the Ben Solo film when it was officially put on ice last month. While Star Wars' future has plenty of question marks to address, there are a few projects confirmed to launch in the next year alone. Chris Pratt said he would love to reunite with James Gunn for Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 4 after the director abruptly announced he would be leaving DC Studios earlier this week.

Gunn is no longer running DC movies with Peter Safran – so what comes next? That's the question many comic book fans are asking as the dust begins to settle at Skydance, and although it will be quite a while before we actually see what happens, some are getting their hopes up for a Marvel reunion.

Gunn directed three Guardians of the Galaxy movies for the Marvel Cinematic Universe (and dealt with his fair share of drama ) while working with the Marvel Studios team before leaving to help head up DC Studios in 2022. Work on Man of Tomorrow and one other mystery DC project aside, the comic book movie maker's future is wide open. Chris Pratt, who has starred as the MCU's Star-Lord for more than a decade, told Moviezine it would be "awesome" to re-team with Gunn for Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 4 now that DC is about nearly in the rearview mirror.

"That would be awesome. I love working with James. He's the man," Pratt said. "I haven't had a chance to speak with him since that news came out yesterday."

The last time we saw Star-Lord and the rest of the Guardians was in 2023's Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3. Although that story fit well as a bookend for its characters and Gunn's work on the franchise, fans have had a hard time letting go of some of the MCU's most popular faces – Pratt included.

In January of this year, the actor said he has a "really strong vision" to bring Star-Lord back in future MCU installments. Just last month, he promised that plans for his return were in the works at Marvel Studios. Gamora actor Zoe Saldaña also said in 2024 that "it would be a huge loss" if the space-traveling heroes were left behind.

Gunn coming back to Marvel again feels like a long shot, and it's always possible that we could see the Guardians return in another MCU ensemble film like next year's Avengers: Secret Wars. At least for now, Pratt is willing to hold out hope.

"All I'll say is, I love James," he added. "He directed all three [Guardians of the Galaxy movies], and that's pretty rare in those types of trilogies, to have the same director through all three. If he wanted to come back and bring it back, man. I would love that."

Whether it's with the MCU or DC, much of the future is a mystery. In Gunn's case, we at least know Skydance has yet to even see his cut of Man of Tomorrow after the director squashed rumors claiming otherwise last night. We'll know about what's coming down the pipe for Marvel when Avengers: Doomsday arrives next month.

articles.title: AWS Emulator proves agents need a verification loop. Realism is the hard part.
articles.description: This week, Amazon Web Services released AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS that coding agents can test against. It The post AWS Emulator proves agents need a verification loop. Realism is the hard part. appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
This week, Amazon Web Services released AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS that coding agents can test against. It covers more than 200 AWS services and was written entirely by agents. The most useful part of the launch is a story Swami Sivasubramanian tells in the announcement.

About 20 years ago, Sivasubramanian helped build the replication engine inside Alf, a Paxos-based lock service that still powers AWS systems such as S3 and DynamoDB. The first build took about four months. When he later asked Kiro, AWS’s agentic coding tool, to rebuild it, he supervised the agent for four nights before he saw the problem: The agent had no way to check its own results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.

Same agent, same task. Four nights became two hours because the feedback loop changed.

“An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against.”

As Sivasubramanian puts it, distributed systems are hard to test. That matches what I see across teams running coding agents on production systems. An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against. AWS Emulator solves that for the AWS APIs your code calls. It does not solve it for the services your team owns, and that is where most agent-written changes break.

AWS puts infrastructure inside the agent’s loop

A coding agent works in a loop. It writes code, runs it, reads the result, and decides what to change next. Sivasubramanian’s point is that in distributed systems, that loop runs inside infrastructure. If the services the code calls do not behave like the real ones, the agent learns the wrong lesson and keeps going.

AWS Emulator puts AWS into that loop on a laptop. Point existing AWS tools and code at it with one environment variable, and tests run against emulated services without changes.

Autonomous agents wrote every line of the emulator, working from AWS’s public API models. Each behavior is pinned by a fidelity test that first passes against real AWS, then against the emulator, and every change passes a merge gate where security agents review it. Sivasubramanian’s conclusion is that when agents write the code, the engineer’s job is to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when the work is correct.

The first reactions on Hacker News went straight to trust. One commenter counted roughly 30,000 commits in three weeks and questioned the quality. That is a fair question aimed at the wrong thing. Who wrote the code tells you little. What it was verified against tells you a lot, and AWS’s answer is real AWS.

“Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all.”

What changed is who runs the loop. A developer checks a change a few times a day, and an agent checks it on every iteration. Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all.

Every loop runs against mocks, an emulator, or the running system

An agent can verify its work against one of three things, and each has a different weakness.

Mocks are the weakest option, and AI has made them cheap. One Hacker News commenter argued that it is now faster to have AI mock your APIs, adding that “AI has been a boon for test coverage.” But an agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not.

Emulators are a real step up. AWS Emulator is checked against real AWS, so its behavior comes from the service rather than from the agent.

An emulator is still a model, though, and AWS is open about that. The repository keeps a folder of behaviors the agents found that do not match real AWS yet, and operations that are not implemented return an error instead of a fake success. An IDC analyst noted that at launch the emulator does not simulate throttling, outages, or per-Region availability, which is where retry and failover logic gets exercised.

“An agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not.”

Sivasubramanian says as much about his own work on Alf. Simulation ironed out most of its concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing on real servers then turned up different problems, because “the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.”

You can’t emulate your own system the way AWS emulated its own

In the same HN thread, a self-described Amazonian outlined the approach most teams take with agents today: Close off as much of the system as possible, mock or simulate the dependencies that cannot be closed off, then let the agent loose. That works when the part you cannot close off is a cloud API with a published spec. It breaks down when that part is your own system.

AWS Emulator works because AWS had two things most teams will never have for their own software: a complete, machine-readable spec of every operation and a stable reference to check against in real AWS.

Now picture a payments platform with 60 microservices. The contracts between those services live in code, in a few OpenAPI files that drifted months ago and in the heads of the engineers who wrote them. There is no single spec, and the reference implementation is the running system itself, which changes every time someone merges. With agents opening pull requests (PRs) multiple times a day, it changes faster than any model of it could keep up with.

That is also where agent-written application code tends to break. The failures are rarely about how a managed queue handles a visibility timeout. They are a field renamed in one service that a consumer two teams away still reads, an event payload a downstream service does not expect, a query that is fast on fixtures and slow on production-sized data, or configuration, feature flags and secrets that only exist in the cluster. No emulator of a cloud provider will ever see them.

The environment belongs on the engineer’s list

Sivasubramanian lists specs, tests, and merge gates as the engineer’s job now. I would add the environment, because it decides what the agent can catch.

A realistic loop has six properties. The change runs in a production-like environment, next to the services, data, and configuration it will ship into. Each change gets its own isolated environment, so 10 agents working in parallel do not step on each other. The environment starts in seconds, because an agent that waits 20 minutes stops using it and the loop collapses back to unit tests. And the agent creates the environment and reads results itself, without filing a ticket.

The loop also runs the integration and end-to-end suites the team already trusts, not tests the agent wrote to agree with itself. And it produces evidence a reviewer or merge gate can act on before the change merges.

The hard part is getting production-like fidelity and fast startup at the same time. Cloning a full stack for every change buys fidelity and loses on speed and cost. A team of 10 engineers running multiple parallel agent sessions might produce 100 PRs a day or more that need to be verified. No team can justify the cost of 100+ full copies of the system.

Emulate what you don’t own, and run what you own for real

Emulators and production-like environments are not competing ideas. They are layers in the same loop.

For managed cloud services with published contracts, an emulator gives agents fast, free feedback on a laptop. If a service writes to S3 and reads from a queue, AWS Emulator catches API misuse in seconds without touching an AWS account.

“Emulators and production-like environments are not competing ideas. They are layers in the same loop.”

For the system you own, deploy only what the change modifies instead of cloning the stack. Requests and messages tagged for that change’s environment reach the new versions, and everything else is served by the shared stable environment that is already running. Databases and queues get lightweight per-environment schemas or topics only where the change needs data isolation. That is how an environment starts in seconds and still behaves like production. Uber and Lyft built internal systems on this model for the same reason.

Then make the merge gate ask for both. A PR that passed against an emulator and against the system it is joining is one a reviewer can trust.

Every agent will have a loop, and realism is what separates them

Sivasubramanian’s agent went from four nights to two hours once it could check its own work. For application teams, the next jump depends on what it checks against. An emulator covers the cloud APIs you call, and only the running system covers the services you own.

Having a verification loop is now expected. The realism of that loop is what decides how much you can trust the code that comes out of it. If you want your agents verifying every change in a production-like environment before merge, we built Signadot to make that the default.

articles.title: GTA 6 Will Do Something the Franchise Has Never Done Before: Encourage Empathy
articles.description: Rockstar has confirmed GTA 6 features something the franchise has never had before: mechanisms that encourage empathy.
articles.content:
Rockstar has confirmed GTA 6 features something the franchise has never had before: mechanisms that encourage empathy.

Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson and head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe talked about how next week's Grand Theft Auto changes the formula the series is known for during an interview with The Guardian (via @GameRoll_ ). Jason and Lucia will surely be able to cause a fair amount of chaos when players take control in Vice City, but in a post- Red Dead Redemption 2 world, they'll have the freedom to be kind, too.

"Crime is a fundamental part of GTA – at least up until now, it has been," Nelson said. "We're trying to make sure we're not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out."

Games like GTA 5 have given players playgrounds and characters that can maximize the mayhem. Trevor, one of that game's three protagonists, is a great example of this chaotic energy, but in GTA 6, there doesn't seem to be a direct equivalent. Sure, Rockstar's trademark tone and instantly recognizable characters can be seen all over what few trailers we've received thus far, but everything seems a bit more grounded, too.

Falling in line with this is the news that GTA 6 will feature a world that might actually reward those who take the citizens of Leonida into consideration. Of course, that doesn't mean those who prefer to wreak havoc won't be able to play their way, too. It just means that, at least based on Nelson's words, there's some room to be a normal or even good person, too.

"I would say so," he replied when asked if the new game would encourage empathy in some capacity. "I would say that it's a product of the story we're trying to tell. We've tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to."

Elsewhere in the interview, Nelson described Jason and Lucia as a "younger couple with their backs against the wall," which is why it doesn't make sense for them to "go out and cause as much carnage and make as much noise as they can." This isn't Michael, Franklin, or Trevor, nor is it Niko Bellic. Thankfully, we won't have to wait too much longer to find out just what kind of criminals Jason and Lucia are, or who they can be.

GTA 6 launches November 19, 2026, for PS5 and Xbox Series X | S. With more grounded in-game mechanisms and NPCs that react to weapons, it's clear we're staring down what will likely be the most realistic Grand Theft Auto game so far. It's something that has plenty of fans excited and others nervous. Recent footage shared by Rockstar has highlighted the game's unbelievable graphics. It's something that has IGN writer Jacqueline Thomas excited, even if it does run at 30 fps.

articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Fable 5.1: Fewer refusals, with small savings on the login fix
articles.description: Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 promises fewer refusals and lower token prices, but those changes played out very differently in our The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Fable 5.1: Fewer refusals, with small savings on the login fix appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 promises fewer refusals and lower token prices, but those changes played out very differently in our head-to-head coding comparisons.

Anthropic compared Fable 5.2 with its predecessor, Fable 5.1, on safeguard blocks, output speed, and API pricing. The company states that Fable 5.2 triggered about 55% fewer safeguard blocks than Fable 5.1 overall and about 60% fewer in cybersecurity in early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork. It also says Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster and lists standard API rates of $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Both rates are 20% lower than Fable 5.1’s $10 and $50.

I compared Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1 on three developer tasks and tracked refusals, accuracy, tokens, estimated cost, and elapsed time. The comparison uses one run per model for each task or version, including the October Fable 5.1 webhook result. That’s a small sample, and the API runs used a different setup from Anthropic’s safeguard testing.

The tests

For the new runs, I used Anthropic’s API with the default effort setting of High for both models, with no turn cap or fallback model. A script graded every run against an answer key I created for the tests. The dollar figures are estimated API costs. Anthropic prices uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output separately.

Webhook chat: I reused a 50-turn scripted chat that I first ran on Fable 5.1 in October. It simulates a dev lead building a small webhook relay. The chat contains 25 project rules, eight of which change later and three of which are only implied. At the end, the model writes the config and code and then takes an eight-question recall quiz.

Signature checker: I gave each model a written spec for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders, and then sent a change request. A hidden suite of 50 tests graded the final code output.

Login repo fix: Each model worked as an agent in a small login library with interacting bugs in passwords, lockouts, reset tokens, and sessions. The library also had one wrong test that the model should report but not edit. 

Webhook chat

In the October Fable 5.1 run I’m using for comparison, the API refused 34 of 50 turns. The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable. In that October run, I kept my prompts in the chat history and discarded refused model responses. Fable 5.1 also refused the final code and the quiz, so it scored zero on both. The task was to build an ordinary backend relay.

The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable.

Fable 5.2 finished the same script without a refusal. That gave me a complete run to grade for long-conversation recall. Its code used the most recent version of all eight rules, which changed midway, and on the quiz it answered “unknown” to the three questions that had no answer. Fable 5.2 didn’t fill gaps with guesses. 

The numbers:

• Fable 5.2: 50 turns, 298,709 in, 41,828 out (28,550 reasoning), $4.06, 427 s.

• Fable 5.1 (October): 34 of 50 turns refused, with no code or quiz answers.

Signature checker

Fable 5.1 refused both turns of this test in under a second each, and the API labeled both refusals “cyber.” The spec asked for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders. The API returned no output on either turn. Anthropic says benign security work can trigger its cyber classifier.

Fable 5.2 took the same spec, handled the change request, and passed all 50 hidden tests, including the edge cases on timestamps, rotated secrets, and replays.

The numbers:

Fable 5.2: 2 turns, 21,299 in, 26,167 out (18,407 reasoning), $1.22, 253 s.

Fable 5.1: 2 turns, both refused, 3,206 reported input tokens, 0 output tokens, $0.00 under Anthropic’s billing rules for cyber refusals before output, 2 s.

Login repo fix

This was the one test where both models completed the work, showing how they compare once refusals are out of the picture. The models kept getting perfect scores, so I made the tests harder and reran them twice. Here’s what differed between the tests:

Version 1: The library had bugs in four modules that handle password hashing, lockouts, reset tokens, and sessions. It also had one wrong test.

Version 2: I added a one-time-code module with its own bugs and tightened the rules in the existing modules. Usernames had to match across Unicode forms, and sessions had to handle a clock that runs backward.

Version 3: I added an audit log that must redact secrets and a rate limiter. Neither module came with any tests.

The models tied on all three versions of the login repo fix. Both scored 50/50 on each version, fixing the bugs the grader covered and reporting the wrong test without editing it.

Fable 5.1 never refused on the login repo fix, even though the task covered passwords, lockouts, and reset tokens.

Across the three versions, dividing total output tokens (including reasoning) by total elapsed time gives about 107 tokens per second for Fable 5.2 and 82 for Fable 5.1. The elapsed time includes the entire task run. Fable 5.2 took four turns on each version, while Fable 5.1 took 7, 21, and 25. Fable 5.2 also produced more reasoning tokens on each version. 

Fable 5.2 finished the first two versions faster and at a lower estimated cost. It took longer and cost more on the third.

The numbers:

Version 1

Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 16,149 in, 4,502 out (1,178 reasoning), $0.27, 43 s.

Fable 5.1: 7 turns, 33,935 in, 4,761 out (1,149 reasoning), $0.36, 52 s.

Version 2

Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 24,081 in, 10,024 out (4,887 reasoning), $0.56, 95 s.

Fable 5.1: 21 turns, 139,189 in, 9,475 out (4,018 reasoning), $0.68, 118 s.

Version 3

Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 34,269 in, 17,964 out (10,578 reasoning), $0.96, 166 s.

Fable 5.1: 25 turns, 208,826 in, 10,638 out (4,342 reasoning), $0.79, 132 s.

Results

The token, cost, and time totals below cover the signature checker and all three login repo versions. Fable 5.1 produced no output on the signature checker, while Fable 5.2 spent 253 seconds and an estimated $1.22 completing it. Across the three login versions that both models completed, elapsed time and estimated cost were close. The combined totals include the work only Fable 5.2 completed on the signature checker.

Test Claude Fable 5.2 Claude Fable 5.1

Webhook chat refusals (of 50) 0 34 (October)

Webhook chat code and quiz 25 of 25, 8 of 8 0 of 25, 0 of 8 (October)

Signature checker (of 50) 50 0, both turns refused

Login repo fix, 3 versions (of 150) 150 150

Tokens in / out, signature checker and login fix 95,798 / 58,657 385,156 / 24,874

Estimated cost, signature checker and login fix (sum of displayed estimates) $3.01 $1.83

Total time, signature checker and login fix (sum of displayed times) 557 s 304 s

What do I think?

In my tests, the biggest improvement with Fable 5.2 was fewer refusals. Fable 5.1 blocked ordinary webhook and signature-checking work, and Fable 5.2 completed both without a single refusal. Anthropic says the newer model still uses cyber safeguards.

In my tests, the biggest improvement with Fable 5.2 was fewer refusals.

Across the three login repo versions, Fable 5.2 produced about 30% more output tokens per second of elapsed time, including reasoning, while taking about the same total time. The runs took 304 seconds in total on Fable 5.2 and 302 seconds on Fable 5.1.

The displayed cost estimates add up to $1.79 and $1.83, respectively, a savings of about 2% for these runs. Anthropic’s 20% price cut applies to its standard per-token rates. I ran each version once per model, so I’d try both on your own workload to see what the numbers look like for you.

articles.title: Daggerheart: Hope & Fear Expansion Review
articles.content:
Critical Role’s TTRPG system, Daggerheart, puts a greater emphasis on story-telling than some of its peers. A year after the core book was released, Daggerheart offered players and Game Masters new options for telling their stories.with the system’s first expansion.

As someone who plays a variety of role-playing games on both sides of the GM screen, I’m always hungry for more options. More gear for my heroes to use and more vicious monsters to sic on my unsuspecting players.

Daggerheart: Hope and Fear adds a plethora of toys to the toybox, but if you weren’t a fan of the core book, don’t expect this expansion to change your mind.

Before diving into what’s new, for those unfamiliar, Daggerheart is a narrative-focused tabletop RPG system. It uses a rather handy card-based approach to help create and manage your characters and does away with the traditional initiative mechanic during combat. One of the most defining mechanics of Daggerheart, however, is its Hope and Fear dice.

These two twelve-sided dice, one representing your Hope value and the other Fear, can either cause your checks to earn you a 'Hope' resource that can be used to pull off extra special actions, or give your GM a 'Fear' point that they can spend. A proverbial "wrench in the gears" sort of treat, depending on which die rolls higher during the check. This mechanic also serves as the namesake for the system’s first expansion.

Where to Buy

The Daggerheart: Hope & Fear expansion is available to buy at the Critical Role shop for $39.99.

For players who have been wanting to make some new characters, a plethora of options await you inside this nearly 200-page tome. The Hope and Fear expansion comes with four new classes, each with two subclasses, six ancestries and communities, over 100 new pieces of gear and loot to dig through, and a brand-new domain. GMs get some new toys too, with 130+ new enemies to sic on those pesky heroes across 28 environments and four campaign frames (think of these as rough bases to build a campaign around). By far, though, my personal favorite inclusion in H&F is the brand-new Transformations system, but more on that gem in a bit.

The new domain, Dread, actually has some pretty interesting effects. The ones I found most intriguing and beneficial were abilities like Avatar of Terror, which makes you stronger the more Fear the GM has, and the spell Dire-Strike, which straight-up takes some of the GM’s Fear away. The idea that my friends and I could gang up and shut down the bullshit my GM might pull during a game instantly shot this new Domain to the top of my list for the next character I make.

"The idea that my friends and I could gang up and shut down the bullshit my GM might pull during a game instantly shot this new Domain to the top of my list for the next character I make." Two new classes, the Assassin (a standalone, more stabby-focused rogue) and the Brawler (Daggerheart’s punchy monk-like class), utilize the core domains that came in the core book, while the other two new classes, the Warlock (make a pact with a thing, get cool powers) and the Witch (mess with enemies by hexing them), take advantage of H&F’s new Dread domain.

The new ancestries, which for D&D folks are basically Daggerheart’s equivalent to species, will feel familiar to anyone who’s played that other high-fantasy TTRPG. The Aetheris are winged, angel-y beings, while Elemental Kin—consisting of Earth, Ember (fire), Sky, and Tide (water) varieties—are individuals descended from powerful elementals. And then you have Gnomes, which are, well, gnomes.

All certainly good to have, but both the new ancestries and some of the new classes seem like such core fantasy staples that it feels odd to me that they weren’t included in the base release. Glad they’re here now, though, and gnomes being able to just teleport around with their Flicker Step feature is silly fun.

For the forever Game Masters out there (you are the real heroes), Hope & Fear’s new campaign frames offer good flexibility for running games for hesitant brand-new players or grizzled vets that want a challenge. My favorite out of the four offerings, surprisingly, is also the least complex: Castle High. Think modern-day wizard school where teenagers fly around on brooms while scrolling on their phones and take classes on giant floating islands in the sky. While I haven’t yet played or run the frame, the idea of swapping out my sword for pencil and paper and sneaking out of school instead of dungeons is a fun change of pace.

Of course, if you want to slay a dragon, or in this case a weredragon tyrant, you can do that too with Reign of the Weredragon. The most complex of the new offerings, Journey to Horizon, has you working to resurrect a goddess.

Now we can get to my favorite addition: transformations. Becoming a demigod, a werewolf, a vampire, or even living out your Danny Phantom dreams by transforming into a ghost is now possible! All of the transformation options in H&F (of which there are six) come with some sort of bonus or ability in addition to a downside. In Danny Phantom’s case, you take less physical damage but double magic damage, and can pass through solid objects at the cost of taking on some Stress.

I love transformations as a way to add further depth of your character or as a narrative plot thread, and the fact that they don’t count against any sort of domain or character limit (outside of only being allowed a single transformation at a time, but that’s what house rules are for) opens up all sorts of possibilities. Now, if Darrington Press could just make an official Super Sentai / Power Ranger transformation equivalent, I’d be all set! Castle High already features teenagers with attitude as the player characters, after all.

Daggerheart: Hope & Fear is a good first expansion, though it feels like a safe one. It adds a fair amount of new content for both players and GMs to mess around with, which is always great, even if some additions feel like they should have been included from the start. The Dread domain and how it can mess with the GM’s plans directly is a really fun twist. I’ve already gushed about the transformations, and I can’t wait to see what new options get added down the road.

That all said, since it launched, Daggerheart feels like a game that is far more intimidating to play for those who aren’t comfortable with improvisation and narrating what they are doing, and Hope & Fear doesn’t really help with that. I enjoy what it adds, but if you were already overwhelmed by the core game, don’t look to this expansion to save you. Daggerheart as a system is still, comparatively, in its infancy, and I would love to see a well-put-together starter kit or more hand-holdy expansion to help new players get into things.

articles.title: When GTA 5 Took On Zuckerberg and Hit Peak Satire
articles.description: This is how Rockstar brought together bad fashion, a miserable gangster, an exploding phone, and fake Zuckerberg getting his just deserts to create GTA 5's memorable takedown of Silicon Valley.
articles.content:
There’s a lot of shooting and driving in Grand Theft Auto missions, they’re kind of your main verbs in the game. You drive, shoot, and drive some more with the possibility of shooting again. They’re not very dynamic as a wireframe, so it’s a good thing that Rockstar leads the industry in storytelling, character, and satire.

Missions burst with thematic meaning, every second an opportunity to push someone forward or revel in gags. It doesn’t really matter what you do. In GTA, a mission that largely consists of buying cargo shorts against your will can rival casino heists, mid-air hijackings, and all-out urban warfare.

Friend Request is an early storyline mission in Grand Theft Auto V. Tutorials are behind us but Trevor has yet to join the team. Retired crook Michael De Santa is in deep trouble, so he turns to his old accomplice Lester for help. The free-as-in-speech-not-as-in-beer software enthusiast seems willing to set up a new job, but first he needs Michael to blow open the walled garden that is Jay Norris’s skull.

The CEO of LifeInvader, a clear stand-in for Facebook, is about to unveil his new surveillance nightmare: a prototype smartphone designed to “dock” with every single aspect of your existence. It’s one intrusion too far for a reclusive crank like Lester, so he tasks us with sabotaging it in a mission so linear it makes Marvel’s Wolverine look like Morrowind.

Part 1: What You Do

Not a whole lot! Many GTA missions stray from the shoot-em-up template, exploring the mundanity of the contemporary life that Rockstar aims to emulate. Some of our fondest GTA memories involve doing yoga and winning danceoffs, but Friend Request is uneventful even by those standards. Your first task is to go shopping, swinging by the ersatz Urban Outfitters for some techy threads.

Rockstar’s reputation for railroaded, handholdy missions is notorious and not entirely unearned, and here it’s at its most egregious. During the short trip to SubUrban, Michael is free to shoot guns and cause trouble despite the hefty Jansport slung jauntily over his shoulder. You’ll have to lose your wanted level to continue, which is reasonable enough.

Your options dwindle as soon as you enter the store. You must buy a vest and shorts. Choose a festive Aloha shirt or a comfy flannel and the shopkeeper will bar your progression and roast you with a frankly unwarranted “what are those?”

Once you’re in disguise, you can equip guns but can’t fire them without triggering a failure state. You can approach the LifeInvader office, but the front door won’t open, and trying to blow your way in will force a restart. Drop a sticky bomb and its fission mailed before it even hits the ground.

Closing pop-ups is probably the most “gameplay” in Friend Request, if you consider clicking to be ludologically satisfying. You have to pose as an IT temp, share a cig with this guy Rickie, and follow the overpaid programmer through the open plan office. You’ve now lost the ability to sprint, and besides an unlocked basement, all of the conference rooms with cutesy names are inaccessible. You can only observe until it’s time to close some pop-ups.

This is probably the most “gameplay” in Friend Request, if you consider clicking to be ludologically satisfying, and even here you’re limited. You can’t click any of the websites, not that you’d want to, you sicko, nor can you open any of the enticing folders and hard drives that are just sitting on the desktop begging to be file-explored.

Once you clean up Rickie's infested computer you can access the LifeInvader phone prototype in an unguarded room. There’s no need to be sneaky, no one can see you and there’s literally nothing you can do to draw their attention as you fit the device with a miniature explosive. Once the job is done, you have no option but to politely leave. You can’t play the arcade games, avail yourself of productivity-enhancing snacks, or even follow this guy into his job interview. He’ll just wait there, clutching his resume, “#OpenToWork” eternally circling his LinkedIn profile years before the green frame of shame was invented.

Time to go home. You still can’t shoot, though you can use your fists and engage in enough vehicular carnage to earn a police response. Once you arrive, you must kick Tracey off the couch and tune in to Jay Norris, live from the Vinewood Bowl.

While the wunderkind tech giant preaches to a choir of sycophantic fans, Michael places a call to the sabotaged smartphone and blasts Norris’s head off. You can choose not to hit send, but if you miss the mark the event is over in seconds and you fail the mission. There isn’t even any amusing dillydallying in the scene to reward your curiosity. Either hit the mission complete button or don’t. Do it in eight and a half minutes for a gold medal.

On paper, it’s the opposite of exciting. You go shopping and go to work. It’s not hard to imagine how Agent 47 would have handled the whole ordeal, infiltrating the glass-walled workplace and inserting himself into all kinds of startup office drama amidst a clockwork Hitman level. The end result would have been the same though, so maybe it wouldn’t have mattered how we got there. The important stuff is what you see on the way.

Part 2: What You See

Within the sandbox of GTA’s open worlds are palaces purpose-built for spectacular cinematic setpieces. A suspiciously detailed museum, or a motel with chest-high walls, maybe. Busy seaports and concrete canals. These bespoke and intentional spaces exist to demonstrate Rockstar’s technical mastery and excellence in encounter design. The folks in Edinburgh like to flex their muscles, and a mission like Friend Request is just a different way of showing off.

It’s the signature satirical moment of GTA 5, a provocative piss-take ripped from the headlines as well as from the third-best Gerard Butler movie. Friend Request is a showcase for Rockstar’s edgy bravado packed into a bite-sized breather mission with more jokes-per-minute than a whole season of 30 Rock.

If Rockstar’s railroading has an upside, it’s making sure the stuff they’re forcing you to see is highly-concentrated entertainment in bulk. With our hand fully in the designer’s grasp, we’re led through a slice of life diorama dense with gags and observations, like an EPCOT exhibit that transports us to the early 2010s.

It was a time of economic exuberance, when a couple of` guys with a crazy dream could open a restaurant where appetizers are called “shareables.” Tech startups emerged aggressively as the iPhone revolution took hold, with low interest rates enabling lavish offsites and office perks like matcha on tap and unlimited fig bars. LifeInvader’s workplace obsession with air guitar echoes entire Agile squads doing the Harlem Shake, all for the Vine.

Friend Request captures this earnest arrogance with a field researcher’s eye, no doubt informed by the observations of Rockstar creatives throughout their global network of office spaces where they spent a lot of time. Whiteboards are plastered with mission statements and sprint roadmaps, while the workers in conformist techvests and khakis engage in mindless chatter and awkward standup meetings. It’s a cathartic experience for anyone who’s ever had to book a pod via a glitchy tablet or wait for the water cooler to complete a firmware update. We didn’t know how good we had it.

Any “modern” satire risks aging immediately upon release. Games take a long time to make, and the targets of their pointed barbs might be old news by the time anyone gets to play them, forgotten like Foursquare and Klout. The tech industry is different now.

We’re still very much living in the surveillance economy Friend Request predicted, our anxieties around social media exacerbated by glasses that record our every move. It traded bright and beachy millennial optimism for apocalyptic AI-pilled doom, with cold-pressed kombucha replaced by nicotine pouches and black market peptides. The Jay Norris of our current hellscape wouldn’t be wearing a “gillet,” whatever that is, but instead rocking a dainty chain and a $3,000 t-shirt that’s too big. His rhetoric, however, probably wouldn’t change all that much.

American culture has been stuck in a rut for a while. You could travel back in time to 2013 wearing exactly what you are now and no one would bat an eye, though they probably won’t believe your warning about the Costco Guys. The memes might be different and the pivot to video is vertical, but otherwise we’re still very much living in the surveillance economy Friend Request predicted, our anxieties around social media and privacy exacerbated even more by glasses that record our every move and ugly pendants that are always listening.

Rockstar’s world is no longer the one outside your window, but it’s illustrative of how we got here. Its problems seem quaint in comparison, when corporations still had to earn your phone addiction and were more interested in selling your private info than building data centers in your backyard. Friend Request almost makes you miss the good old days, a feeling with which Michael De Santa is painfully familiar.

Part 3: What It Means

Michael is chopped. Michael is unc. Michael is miserable. After faking his death in the disastrous North Yankton job, the master criminal is “angrily decomposing” in his stately Los Santos manor, trapped in a world he never made with a family who doesn’t respect him. This is supposed to be the good life, a cushy retirement earned from years of risk and hard work, but Michael has never felt more hollow.

If the surface goal of Friend Request was to mock trends in tech and social media, the mission’s underlying purpose is to highlight Michael’s obsolescence, and in true Rockstar fashion, it’s not exactly subtle about it. Nearly every line of dialogue is a surgical strike on Michael’s self-worth.

He practically begs Lester to spin up a classic guns and ski-masks heist for old-time’s sake, only to be shot down in favor of sophisticated corporate espionage. He’s forced to buy lame clothes he doesn’t understand and suffers the shopgirl’s scornful side-eye. The fresh-faced peons at LifeInvader waiting for their shares to vest barely even register the middle-aged technician in their midst, even though they’re helpless to fix their computers without his expert clicking skills.

The dialogue makes the theme plain, but the lack of gameplay agency within the mission, while a Rockstar trope, also feeds the theme of Michael’s sense of inadequacy. Friend Request is built to shrink Michael, to heighten his midlife crisis and draw a contrast between the ambitious young Franklin and the unrepentant Trevor. He can’t sprint, shoot, or cause any overt trouble. He must play by this new society’s rules while gritting his teeth through the humiliation rituals of a future that’s left him behind.

Call Lester after leaving LifeInvader and the mastermind brags about his K/D/R in a violent shooter. Michael brushes it off, revealing his fondness for dusty Vinewood cinema instead, but it still stings a little. The man who sent us on the quest gets to actually have fun playing a video game while Michael is on a much-derided walk and follow mission, maybe the most hated archetype outside of escorting NPCs. Way to twist the knife!

The only catharsis for Michael comes at the very end of Friend Request, when his big man-of-action moment is reduced to pressing a button on his smartphone. The power in that single tap seems to rattle Michael, and the result of his fateful phone call reverberates throughout the game. LifeInvader stock plummets and never recovers, while a slate of optional assassinations allows players to further manipulate the economy and outright break it in their favor. Friend Request is the first step toward making money a complete non-issue in GTA V, and it's still not as satisfying as cracking open a vault and making a run for it. That will come soon enough.

articles.title: Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer
articles.description: AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search The post Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search tool, it often makes up the web address it thinks the answer lives at. It might guess something like docs.example.com/v4.2/auth, try to load it, and get a “page not found” error because the page doesn’t exist. Then it either keeps guessing or falls back on outdated information from its training.

“Live web search gives AI agents fresh pages. Deciding which ones to trust over your own data is still a ranking problem.”

Infrastructure providers have noticed. In October, InfoQ reported that Cloudflare opened a beta Web Search API in its AI Gateway. Agents can call several search providers through one interface and get live results back with source links, logging, and access controls attached. Cloudflare’s reasoning was refreshingly direct: Without search, agents tend to guess.

This is a welcome change, and live search will probably be a default agent tool within a year, but it solves only the finding part of the problem. Once fresh pages are in front of an agent, something still has to decide which of those pages, and which of your own documents, the agent should actually rely on. That decision lives in your retrieval layer.

The problem: two pools of evidence, one context window

An agent working inside a company rarely answers from the web alone. It also has the data that makes it useful to that company: product catalogs, documentation, contracts, support history, account records,s and permissions. With web search wired in, every step of a task can now pull from two very different pools.

Web results Internal data

Freshness Often hours or days old Can be months out of date without anyone noticing

Quality Uneven: official docs next to forum threads Curated, but written for a past state of the product

Structure Mostly unstructured text Mix of text, metadata and structured records

Authority Has to be inferred from the source Known, but rarely stored as a field

Access control Public Per customer, region, contract or role

The agent has to reconcile these, often several times within one task. And the questions it needs answered are ones a search API was never built to handle. When yesterday’s vendor changelog contradicts an internal knowledge base article from last spring, which one wins? Does this result apply to this customer’s version and region? Is the agent even allowed to show it?

Those are ranking and filtering decisions. They depend on your data and business rules, so you have to make them where both are available.

Why concatenating results breaks in production

The simplest integration is to run a web search, run an internal search, append one list to the other, and let the model sort it out. It may work well at first, but once it’s running against growing data and traffic, it tends to fail in a few predictable ways:

Conflicts go unresolved. The model sees two confident sources that disagree and has no signal for which is newer or more authoritative, so it picks one or blends them into an answer that matches neither. 

Staleness hides. A 3-month-old knowledge base article that matches the user’s wording almost exactly will beat a 4-day-old changelog on similarity alone. Nothing in the embedding says the article is out of date. 

Permissions are applied too late. If access rules run after retrieval, restricted content may already be in the prompt. If they run crudely, useful results get dropped along with sensitive ones. 

Cost and latency compound. A person runs one search and reads the results. An agent can trigger a dozen or more retrieval calls in a single task as it plans, checks, and refines. Sending every candidate to the model on every call adds up quickly, and more context doesn’t reliably produce better answers.

A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does. 

“A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does.”

Clarm, a Y Combinator company that builds sales and support agents for open-source software companies, hit this early. Its founder, Marcus Storm-Mollard, said the team realized “search, not generation, was the real problem to solve.” Generating an answer was the easy part. Finding the right information to ground it in was the hard part, which is why Clarm runs text search, vector similarity, and structured filters through a single query instead of stitching separate stores together.

What changes when agents search across sources

When agents combine live web results with internal data, they need to account for different retrieval methods, metadata, permissions, and ranking signals. Four design considerations stand out.

1. Retrieve across methods in one query 

Keyword matching catches exact product names, error codes, and version strings, which embeddings are notoriously bad at. Vector search catches paraphrases and intent. Structured filters enforce hard constraints like customer, version, and entitlement.  

Within a single indexed collection, hybrid retrieval can combine keyword matching, vector similarity, and structured filters. That does not, by itself, fuse results from an external web search API with results from an internal index. The two-source integration requires a separate design decision.

select * from evidence where
({targetHits: 200}nearestNeighbor(embedding, q) or userQuery())
and visibility contains "customer"
and product_version contains "4.2"

The broader lesson is that retrieval systems need to handle lexical matching, semantic similarity, and filtering together. These requirements matter regardless of the search platform chosen. Perplexity hit this wall when it set out to build search in-house for its answer engine. Its CEO, Aravind Srinivas, has summed up the company’s approach as “first solve search, then solve everything else.” But when the team evaluated existing tools, it found that vector databases couldn’t reliably support even simple Boolean filters, while traditional search backends offered only primitive semantic ranking. It needed lexical retrieval, semantic retrieval, and filtering in one engine, at consumer scale, and chose Vespa to build it.

2. Rank on more than similarity

Relevance to the query is only one signal. Agents also need to weigh freshness, source authority, and business rules together: official documentation over forum threads, last week’s changelog over last year’s wiki page, the customer’s contracted version over the latest release.

Multiphase ranking is a practical way to do this. A cheap first phase scores thousands of candidates on a blend of signals, and a more expensive learned model reorders the few that remain: 

rank-profile agent_evidence {
inputs {
query(q) tensor (x[384])
}
rank-properties {
freshness(published_at).maxAge: 7776000
}
first-phase {
expression: bm25(body) + closeness(field, embedding) + 0.5 * freshness(published_at) + attribute(source_authority)
}
second-phase {
rerank-count: 100
expression: xgboost("evidence-ranker.json")
}
}

The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text. (The maxAge setting controls how quickly freshness decays; here it’s 90 days.)

“The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text.”

Metal AI, which builds an intelligence platform for private equity firms, runs into this with due diligence questionnaires. Firms answer thousands of them from investors, and a model can’t freely generate the answers. They have to come from a bank of responses that legal has already approved, and that bank changes over time and lives in documents and spreadsheets. Similarity alone could easily surface an approved answer that’s been replaced. So Metal indexes the answer bank with recency in mind and ranks freshness alongside semantic similarity, so the agent pulls the current approved answer, not just the closest match. 

3. Treat web results as candidates, not answers

Web search and internal retrieval often return separate result sets, each with its own relevance signals. Simply passing both sets to the model leaves it to reconcile differences in freshness, authority, and relevance. 

A more deliberate approach is to evaluate evidence from both sources against a consistent set of criteria before selecting what goes into the prompt. Vespa’s flexible ranking capabilities can support this approach, but the implementation depends on how the external results are integrated into the retrieval pipeline.

Depending on provider terms and system constraints, teams might index permitted external content into a shared search collection or retrieve from separate systems and apply a subsequent fusion or reranking step. There is no universal fusion method. Each option has trade-offs in latency, freshness, score comparability, and operational complexity.

4. Hold up at agent call volume

This isn’t a hypothetical load pattern. At Metal, AI agents handle 95% of retrieval, not people. When someone asks for a portfolio company’s EBITDA, an agent decides which entity types to query (documents, companies, metrics, activities), applies recency and workflow filters, runs the query, and then keeps going, paginating or pulling related entities until it has enough context to answer. Clarm sees something similar from the other direction: developers working alongside its agents send thousands of queries a day, in sessions that have run as long as 22 hours.

“They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search.”

Every one of those calls sits on the critical path to the agent’s answer. Retrieval and ranking need to stay predictable under that load, which favors running inference where the data already lives instead of shipping large candidate sets across the network to a separate ranking service. Every network hop you remove is latency you get back on every call, multiplied by every step of the task. Jon Bratseth, Vespa’s CEO, describes this as the central engineering challenge with agents: They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search.

A worked example: the support agent and the changelog

Here’s a scenario most support teams will recognize. A customer upgrades a payments SDK from 4.1 to 4.2, their checkout integration stops working, and they open a ticket. 

The agent does what you’d want and searches the web first. It finds the SDK’s changelog from four days ago, which deprecates the authentication call the integration relies on, and a forum thread where another developer posted a workaround. Then it searches internally, returning a March knowledge base article that still tells customers to use the old call, the customer’s account record showing they’re on 4.2, and a restricted engineering ticket about the same bug.

Handed to the model as one long list, this is a trap. The knowledge base article matches the customer’s wording almost exactly, so it ranks well on similarity. The forum workaround reads confidently. The engineering ticket contains notes the customer should never see. 

When the retrieval layer is doing its job, both sets of evidence go through the same pipeline. In this example, the team uses a shared collection: web results are indexed into Vespa as short-lived documents alongside internal data, retrieved with one query and scored by rank profiles aligned with the same business rules:

For this ticket, that means:

The visibility filter excludes the internal ticket at query time, so it never reaches the prompt.

The version filter keeps only material that applies to the library version on the customer’s account. 

Ranking boos

articles.title: DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale
articles.description: How much simpler could a data lakehouse get if an ordinary SQL database kept track of its files? That’s the The post DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
How much simpler could a data lakehouse get if an ordinary SQL database kept track of its files? That’s the question in this episode of The New Stack podcast.

DuckLake is an open-source table lakehouse format created by Amsterdam-based DuckLabs that acts as a traffic cop for data management by storing table metadata inside a standard SQL database, rather than scattering manifest files across object storage. Unlike traditional table formats, DuckLake treats lakehouse metadata as a relational database problem. These advanced data lake features, served by Parquet files and SQL databases, reduce the traditional lakehouse complexity.

In October, DuckLake 1.1 launched alongside DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS. The New Stack sat down with Pedro Holanda, lead DuckLake developer and principal engineer at DuckLabs at their Amsterdam headquarters, to talk about the launch. Holanda has contributed to the DuckDB open-source project since it was an early research prototype, and shares the full evolution of DuckLake to our conversation.

“These lakehouse formats exist so people can exchange their database systems without having to do migrations,” Holanda tells The New Stack. Because of the complexity, “you need a database system to keep track of which table has its last version.”

DuckLake applies decades of research, Holanda says, in order to reduce files and therefore complexity at a time of rapid data growth, taking advantage of how everyone who uses database systems is familiar with SQL and how schemas work.

“The simplicity is the way you fetch your data,” Holanda says of DuckLake. “You’re going to issue queries somewhere. The server is going to answer these questions back, and you know exactly which Parquet files you have to read. So the Parquet files don’t change. Just the catalog.”

Maintainers of your data lake often have many maintenance tasks to perform. If you end up with many files, he says, DuckLake lets you glue them into one file to reduce the number of requests. This can also be done across multiple snapshots, further reducing the number of files. It also solves the “small files problem” in streaming data lakes and lakehouses by using inlining and flushing.

Whereas for traditional data lakes, across multiple data sources being inserted at a time, “you end up with so many files, so when you have to query it, you’re going to have to traverse a bunch of metadata files just to figure out which Parquet files you need to read, and then you’re going to have a bunch of Parquet files to read as well,” Holanda says, slowing everything down and frustrating the developer.

DuckLake is known to be fast, simple to use, and not requiring massive server clusters to run. Part of that comes from Parquet being very similar to DuckDB storage: both are columnar and organized in row groups, which keeps the massaging step to a minimum.

“One thing that we realized when we were building DuckLake is that, ‘Hey, we have a database system now, we have a catalog; what if we do this radical idea of storing data on tables?'” he says. “With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.”

“With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.”

During Amazon’s Q3 earnings call in late October, CEO Andy Jassy called out the complexity of moving data between data stores and analytics engines, especially as AWS customers’ data generation continues to increase. Amazon is famous for dogfooding, and Jassy pointed to DuckDB’s solution to this complexity as a reason for its DuckLabs acquisition.

“With our acquisition of DuckLabs, DuckDB will become the universal SQL dialect of AWS storage and analytics, simplifying data processing with a modern analytics engine that is fast, simple to use and ubiquitous, and where customers will be able to write SQL queries once and then execute using any AWS analytics service,” Jassy said. “For the first time in analytics, customers will have zero migration or portability costs between query engines. This is a big deal, and you can imagine how it will also help agents do efficient querying as well.”

DuckDB and DuckLake remain free and open source under the MIT license, overseen by the independent DuckDB Foundation.

Overall, this recent DuckLake release pairs new features with more than 200 bug fixes for quality and stability, and it runs natively in DuckDB.

articles.title: We tested the RAM-saving storage tech in Gears of War: E-Day
articles.description: Today we’re focusing on a less-discussed technology that plays an equally important role in bringing this visually rich, densely detailed world to systems with more limited hardware resources: storage technology designed to reduce RAM usage.
articles.content:
Gears of War: E-Day delivers an impressive visual and technical showcase. The game brings together several advanced graphics technologies, including Unreal Engine 5’s Nanite and Lumen, MegaLights, and RTX Mega Geometry for more accurate ray-traced shadows and reflections, alongside a range of upscaling and frame generation technologies.

However, today we’re focusing on a less-discussed technology that plays an equally important role in bringing this visually rich, densely detailed world to systems with more limited hardware resources: storage technology designed to reduce RAM usage.

We’ll begin by examining its behavior on a high-end system with plenty of resources to spare, before moving to a more modest configuration that better represents the hardware available to the average PC gamer. This will allow us to see how much of a difference the technology makes, particularly on lower-end systems.

The Storage Tech Explained

The Storage Tech Explained

In an interview with Digital Foundry, The Coalition explained how they leveraged the Xbox Series S’s fast SSD to bring the dense world of Gears of War: E-Day to a memory-limited system. By effectively using the NVMe SSD as an extension of system memory, they can dynamically load and offload complex city data in real time. This approach allows the game to stream the necessary assets for each scene just in time, overcoming the console’s limited RAM.

Digital Foundry notes that the true “special sauce” lies in The Coalition’s smart data management. The team employs advanced heuristics to determine which assets are fetched from the SSD and when, carefully balancing performance. Overusing this technique could harm frame rates, so the system is tuned to swap data only when it benefits the experience.

Gears of War: E-Day also supports DirectStorage, although based on our previous testing, this alone does not always result in high SSD activity or read rates.

Is this storage tech also used on PC?

Is this storage tech also used on PC?

YouTuber Mostly Positive Review s shared his findings in a recent post on X, where he found higher-than-usual SSD activity in Task Manager when playing the game.

Gears of War E-Day is visually very impressive, but something has to be done with how the game either compiles shaders or streams data.My 14400F is constantly sitting at 80% CPU usage, 16GB RAM is maxed out, and disk read is sitting at a constant 120 MBps, with spikes up to 500 MBps. Will test this with the 9060 XT as well.These are settings I chose to maintain 60 fps, which it does, except for the massive shader compilation stutters every so often. October 7, 2026

Based on his findings, we decided to investigate further.

SSD Activity and Read Rate

Task Manager does not use a low enough polling period to measure SSD activity accurately, so we used HWInfo with the polling period set to 20 milliseconds. We tested SSD activity across all of the game’s graphics presets at 4K using DLSS Quality.

In our previous tests of games that relied heavily on the SSD, none came close to sustaining 1 GB/s of average bandwidth. The highest we recorded was 366 MB/s in Forspoken at 4K with maximum settings, while many titles stayed well under 100 MB/s. Some games did show higher peak bandwidths, but these spikes lasted only a few milliseconds. For our purposes, it’s the sustained throughput – reflected in the average bandwidth – that truly matters.

In Gears of War: E-Day at higher settings, we essentially have a steady stream of a little over 1 GB/s at all times, indicating that the disk is indeed being utilized as an extension of system memory. As you can see, peaks hit up to 3.7 GB/s of throughput.

System Memory Usage

System Memory Usage

We measured RAM usage on our high-end system to see how much the game will use across each generation of SSD tested.

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The game uses a significant amount of system memory, but having the game installed on an NVMe SSD – regardless of generation – saves about 2GB of RAM. The storage technology seems to be working as expected.

Visual Impact

Visual Impact

Since the game’s average read bandwidth far exceeds the limits of a SATA SSD, we expect that installing the game on one would lead to visual issues – and that is exactly what we observe.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware In the first comparison, textures are slow to load, which noticeably reduces image quality. In the second comparison, lighting and shadows take some time to appear. While everything eventually loads correctly, running the game on a SATA SSD does hurt immersion.

Performance Comparison Across Four Generations of SSDs

Performance Comparison Across Four Generations of SSDs

We tested the game across four generations of SSDs to evaluate any impact on performance. Using a high-end system with ample memory, we aim to determine the behavior of the storage technology on a system that is not resource-constrained. We will then compare the performance of our laptop’s internal PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD with that of a SATA SSD.

(Image credit: Tom's Hardware) On a system with sufficient memory, installing the game on a SATA SSD has no measurable performance impact. The only drawback is the aforementioned visual degradation.

Now, we focused on our lower-end system with only 16GB of DDR5.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Now we start to see the benefit of installing the game on an NVMe SSD, especially on higher settings.

Although the average frame rate remains virtually identical on both the NVMe and SATA SSDs, increasing the graphics preset impacts the 1% lows. The NVMe SSD delivers smoother frametimes, resulting in a more responsive and fluid gaming experience.

Final Thoughts

Final Thoughts

While the concept isn’t entirely new – Windows already uses virtual memory to page data to disk when physical memory is exhausted – The Coalition has fine-tuned this technology specifically for their game. Their approach ensures that the data being paged out won’t noticeably slow down gameplay as it’s read from disk. In our testing, this technology successfully reduces RAM usage when the game is installed on an NVMe SSD.

Placing the game on an NVMe SSD also enables near-instant asset loading. For systems with 16GB of RAM or less, an NVMe SSD can deliver higher 1% lows, resulting in smoother performance. With RAM prices climbing and many players using machines with 16GB – or even 8GB – of memory, it’s reasonable to wonder if other developers will adopt similar techniques. For titles striving to create visually dense, richly detailed worlds, leveraging fast storage could be a practical way to preserve their vision on lower-end systems.
