articles.title: Anthropic wants you to build on Claude. There’s a catch.
articles.description: Anthropic wants developers to build businesses on Claude, but its expansion into enterprise software is raising concerns among founders that The post Anthropic wants you to build on Claude. There’s a catch. appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Anthropic wants developers to build businesses on Claude, but its expansion into enterprise software is raising concerns among founders that the company supplying their models could eventually become their biggest competitor.

A nervous warning to wrappers

Gerald Zingraf, president and COO of GlacierGrid, raised the concern on LinkedIn following Anthropic’s Tuesday expansion of Claude’s enterprise lineup, comparing its strategy to Amazon’s private-label business.

“Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies,” Zingraf writes, drawing on his experience selling products he designed through Amazon before watching the retailer introduce competing products.

“Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies,”

His concern is that Anthropic can see which third-party integrations customers use most frequently and potentially draw on that information when deciding which capabilities to build itself.

“Anthropic has the same view,” he argues, although he offers no evidence that the company uses integration data to identify competitors or inform its product roadmap. For some developers, the risk is no longer hypothetical.

When partners become rivals

Scott Stevenson, CEO of legal AI startup Spellbook, described what happened when Anthropic moved into his company’s market in a November 2 interview with Forbes.

Spellbook uses Claude models for everything from reviewing contracts and suggesting revisions to automating legal workflows. Stevenson recalls Anthropic employees assuring him the company had no plans to compete directly in legal software, before Anthropic launched Claude for Legal, which includes contract-review capabilities that overlap with Spellbook’s business.

“Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,”

“Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,” Stevenson said in the interview. “Ultimately this is inevitable.”

Spellbook hasn’t abandoned Claude. Anthropic still features the startup as a customer, reporting roughly 530,000 monthly contract reviews performed by its Claude-powered agents, while Stevenson also appears in Anthropic’s October 28 announcement of legal artifacts.

The relationship illustrates a difficult position for developers whose products depend on frontier models. Spellbook still benefits from Anthropic’s technology, even as Anthropic develops applications aimed at some of the same customers. Nothing in Stevenson’s account establishes that Anthropic used Spellbook’s proprietary information to develop its legal offering.

When the platform ships your product

Tech founder and Dalton Mills CEO Todd Saunders made a similar argument in a March 10 post on X, following Anthropic’s introduction of Claude Code Review.

“Anthropic is the new Amazon,”

“Anthropic is the new Amazon,” Saunders writes, warning developers building on Claude’s SDK that the company could observe application usage and eventually incorporate competing functionality into Claude.

The company’s November 10 announcement introduced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, while previewing Claude Meetings. Expanded interactive connectors also let partners embed applications directly inside Claude, including software from Adobe and Atlassian.

What the policies leave unsaid

Anthropic has access to information about how customers interact with third-party apps and services, something the company acknowledges in its privacy policy, effective September 10, 2026. What isn’t clear is whether Anthropic looks at which integrations are most popular when deciding what to build next.

The rules are different for business customers. Under Anthropic’s commercial terms, customers retain rights to their inputs and own their outputs, while Anthropic agrees not to use their content to train its models. Its commercial privacy documentation also says feedback data excludes content pulled through connectors, including local and remote MCP servers, unless users paste it directly into a conversation.

Neither document settles how Anthropic uses aggregated integration data.

The tradeoff developers accept

The company is still encouraging developers to build on Claude. It’s just that access to its growing enterprise customer base comes with a tradeoff, since Anthropic controls the interface and can introduce competing features without consulting the developers who depend on it.

For now, Anthropic is asking developers to trust it as both a technology provider and a business partner, even as it moves into markets those same developers are trying to build businesses in. Whether that relationship remains sustainable may depend less on what Anthropic promises today than on what it decides to ship next.

The New Stack has contacted Anthropic for comment and has not received a response.

articles.title: Malaysia plans new law using data center power consumption to catch AI GPU smugglers
articles.description: Malaysia plans to track AI GPU imports and data center power consumption to combat chip smuggling. But will it be able to do so?
articles.content:
Malaysia plans to introduce a new law requiring data center operators to disclose their AI accelerator imports and power consumption to prevent diversion of restricted hardware to countries like China and optimize the use of the country’s power infrastructure, reports Malay Mail. The authorities also plan to charge data center operators for unused electricity capacity they reserve. While the idea to use power consumption to detect potential GPU smuggling has merit, it also has flaws.

Malaysia's Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani acknowledged on Thursday that some companies had rented space in Malaysian data centers to import GPUs legally, which they then shipped abroad in smuggling operations. To prevent such practices, Malaysia's Digital Ministry is now reviewing existing legislation to determine whether local authorities can take action against entities that re-export processors subject to U.S. export bans. The minister stressed that Malaysia wants AI accelerators imported into the country to be used domestically.

The proposed legislation will require data center operators to disclose the number of GPUs they import, their power consumption (presumably nameplate power consumption), the physical locations of their facilities, and the identities of operators and hyperscale customers. The government intends to track data center operations throughout their lifetime rather than limit oversight to the project approval stage.

Meanwhile, data center operators will have to pay for all the electricity capacity they reserve, irrespective of their actual power consumption. For example, if a data center secures 100 MW of power capacity but only uses 50 MW, its operator will still have to pay for the remaining 50 MW. The measure is meant to discourage companies from reserving electricity capacity they may not need for another one to three years. As an added bonus, the measure will further discourage rerouting AI hardware to China while pretending it is used in Malaysia.

While data on power consumption could help Malaysian authorities spot suspicious discrepancies between AI GPU imports and actual data center operations, it is virtually impossible to accurately determine the number of AI accelerators deployed at a facility based on power consumption alone. For example, Nvidia's H100 and H200 SXM GPUs are rated at 700W, whereas its B200 SXM accelerators are rated at 1,000W, yet neither necessarily consumes its rated power under actual workloads.

Furthermore, without knowledge of server configurations, the power consumption of CPUs, memory, storage, and networking equipment, or the power usage effectiveness (PUE) of a particular facility, any estimates of the number of operational GPUs would be imprecise, to put it mildly. Also, there may be a considerable delay between GPU imports and their actual deployment. As a result, reliable verification would require physical inventory audits or other mechanisms to track individual processors.

Johari said that Malaysian authorities were prepared to cooperate with their U.S. counterparts and provide information about facilities that house particular GPUs upon request. However, the minister did not specify whether the new legislation would require data center operators to disclose GPU models and serial numbers, or whether authorities would conduct on-site inspections.

Malaysia has emerged as a major destination for data center investments in Southeast Asia as cloud service providers and AI infrastructure companies expand their presence in the region. To date, Malaysian authorities have approved 117 data center projects, 55 of which are already operational, according to Johari. The proliferation of local AI data centers makes Malaysia a suitable venue for rerouting restricted hardware to countries like China, as it is easier to hide a needle in a pile of needles than in a haystack.

articles.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
articles.description: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for
articles.content:
Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life.

Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely.

But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free  Decoder  wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor.

Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble.

So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder.

Thanks so much. Great to be here.

I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.”

Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET?

It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019.

Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI.

Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff.

Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys.

The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.”

It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like?

It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do.

AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well.

I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world.

In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth.

What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years.

Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff?

Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment.

The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way.

In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close.

There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective.

I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.”

With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day.

I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning?

They put in some of that work in 2023. I think this year we’re seeing another big wave of interest and people making the time and making the headspace to get smarter on it. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for.

In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?”

We’re going to see. There’s a whole bunch of new people. I imagine you have a new cast of characters to go and brief about the technology and what it’s capable of. We’ll see if they have revitalized the institutions.

[Laughs] I’m sure it’ll be all fixed overnight.

They’re very excited today, but we’ll see how it goes. The other thing that I want to ask you about is the technology itself, the nature of the technology itself, and how you are thinking about it, and the nature of the companies that are making the technology.

The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. My favorite example of this is we have straight-up asked Anthropic if it thinks Claude is alive and the answer was not no. The answer was a long discursion into the nature of the word “alive.”

Well, it depends on what you mean by “alive” to start with.

It does. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood? It wasn’t us. Why are we talking about the requirement of flesh and blood to be alive?” And then some further conversation about the moral status of Claude is yet to be determined.

There’s a huge divergence here between the AI overviews most people experience in Google search and “the moral status of Claude is uncertain.” Where are you? How are you situated in that debate?

A big part of how I see our role at CSET as an organization, and then also my role as someone who is cr

articles.title: Researchers allege DeepSeek, Kimi, and other Chinese AI models were trained using banned Nvidia Blackwell GPUs
articles.description: Researchers pinpoint that DeepSeek, Kimi, and other Chinese AI models were trained on export-controlled Nvidia Blackwell chips — statistical analysis on model weights reveals high correlation to Nvidia hardware
articles.content:
The topic of U.S. trade controls precluding the export of Nvidia and AMD high-end AI accelerator chips to China has taken a few twists lately. Jensen Huang's affairs aside, it's an open secret in the industry that Nvidia's Blackwell silicon finds its way into China, whether physically or virtually. UnemploymentLabs, an independent research outfit, has come up with strong evidence that those chips were used for training open-weight Chinese AI models, including DeepSeek V4, Kimi K3.1, MiniMax-M3, and Ling-3.1-Flash.

The scientists are careful to hedge their findings, noting that while their math checks out, it does not reveal where the chips were, how they were accessed, or prove that export controls were broken. As far as we can tell, it's currently not illegal for Chinese companies to rent Blackwell hardware abroad, and even though Nvidia's grip is tightening, U.S. companies aren't strictly prohibited from doing so, as evidenced by the recent Tencent-Oracle deal.

This identification method is limited to models with open weights, and depends on both hardware and software stacks used for model training — and yet it's both clever and simple, like the Egg of Columbus.

(Image credit: UnemploymentLabs) Let's establish some base facts. First, different AI accelerator families have unique counts of shader modules (SMs), marginally analogous to CPU cores — Nvidia's Hopper chips have 132, Blackwell B series have 148, and Blackwell GBs come with 152. Second, while there's more than one software stack for training AI models, PyTorch and its CUDA-aware friends are by far the most widely used on the green team's hardware.

The first step for training a model is initializing its weights, or how strongly the model considers each individual input. In modern LLM architectures, their initialization goes through a randomization step in which their values are adjusted plus/minus pseudo-randomly, using cuRAND — as in, randomly, but a seed starting value results in the same adjustment figures every time.

As you'd expect, doing this for an entire model is a lot of computational work, so this process is spread out across all the SMs, further subdivided into threads. For large weight sets, the thread count per SM is 2,048 for Blackwell and Hopper silicon, and it's surely carefully chosen and optimized for.

The researchers repeated a facsimile of the initialization process using the same chips, software, and thread counts. Using relatively simple statistical analysis, they spotted that their final statistical distribution of weight values precisely matched that of DeepSeek, Kimi, et al. As a test, they changed the SM and thread counts, and predictably, the correlation completely broke down.

This let them pick out each family of Blackwell/Hopper chip used for each model, and eventually they also figured out an approximate count of cards used. They cannot, however, pinpoint which exact variation produced the weights, as this analysis is linked to initialization layout counts alone, thus SM count and usage pattern — not to VRAM capacity, memory bandwidth, or other characteristics that distinguish individual cards.

What about AMD cards like the MI300X, or other silicon with a high enough SM count, using the same software stack? The scientists say that it's not impossible that an AMD card could be set up to show up as two groups of 152 or 148 shaders, although we imagine there'd be little reason to do so. Nevertheless, for DeepSeek V4, they also ruled out that possibility by analyzing the actual weight values themselves, and found that AMD cards still didn't produce the same weight value pattern.

articles.title: Contractor turns a Milwaukee Hackzall into a portable Ethernet untwister after facing job requiring 50,000 custom Cat6 cables
articles.description: This Ethernet cable untwisting tool could cut halve the time needed to install an RJ45 connector.
articles.content:
A contractor faced a project that required them to create 50,000 custom Cat6 cables from scratch, requiring 100,000 Cat6 terminations. The contractor, who goes by Analytical Horsepower on YouTube, had used a large, rare tool to streamline the job, but afterward he decided to build his own portable tool by modifying a Milwaukee Hackzall, cutting the time to straighten the twisted pairs to under two seconds.

His first solution to the problem was to buy a “Wire Straightening Machine” from Alibaba for $500. It does the job well enough, but it’s an industrial machine designed for tabletop use, requiring an AC power source for the power brick and compressed air to run. The concept is that it clamps the wire between two rubber grips using air pressure, and then a linkage converts the rotary motion of the motor into a linear one, allowing the grip to untwist the cable. Since he wanted to use the machine in the field, he needed to make the thing portable — so he disassembled the entire thing, replaced the DC power brick with a 20V DeWalt battery with an adapter, added a push-button switch for power control, and a portable bike pump to deliver compressed air on the go.

It worked well at first, but he soon discovered that it was too bulky to use in the tight and hard-to-reach places where Ethernet cables sometimes terminate, like when you’re installing this heavy-duty outdoor Wi-Fi 7 access point. So, he studied the concept — it involved two flat, grippy surfaces grabbing the twisted cables and then moving back and forth. The back-and-forth motion of the surfaces causes the cables to untwist, with the clamping force ensuring that it remains in contact with the cables as they become flatter.

With this, he realized that he did not need such a bulky machine to do the job — he just needed a reciprocating tool that could accept a clamp. He first looked at a reciprocating saw, but he found that it still had the same bulky problem and also called it “not overly precise.” But when he looked at the Milwaukee Hackzall, he found that it offered the perfect balance of portability and precision. More importantly, it came with a detailed data sheet, instruction manual, and parts breakdown that allowed him to accurately 3D print the plastic parts and laser-cut and bend the metal parts he needed to build his machine. He also used a toggle clamp to hold the Cat6 cable in place instead of a pneumatic piston, which further simplified the machine and cut its size and weight.

After a few steps of trial and error, especially in the quality of the grippy materials used for the clamping surfaces, he finally got it to work. He could reliably untwist softer copper-clad aluminum cables in one go in under two seconds. Harder 100% pure copper conductors, sometimes called solid copper or pure bare copper Ethernet cables, must be untwisted pair-by-pair, though, requiring a bit more time, but it’s still undoubtedly much faster and more convenient than doing the job with just your bare hands.

This tool isn’t worth it if you only untwist a few Ethernet cables every month or so, like this telephone-to-gigabit internet conversion job. But if you’re facing a massive job like Analytical Horsepower, that half a minute you save with every cable end could translate to over 830 cumulative hours of labor saved on the jobsite. It’s a great first-generation tool, with its practical use apparent in the YouTube video. Some commenters suggest extending the toggle clamp handle to reach the trigger so activating the tool is easier, while it also looks like a good idea if there’s a way to incorporate the entire system into a crimper.

articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill
articles.description: Anthropic is positioning its new model, Claude Fable 5.2, for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill appeared first on The New Stack .
articles.content:
Anthropic is positioning its new model, Claude Fable 5.2, for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on Nov. 9 and reported higher scores than OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on two coding benchmarks. Fable 5.2 also has lower standard API rates.

Anthropic’s launch benchmarks put Fable 5.2 ahead of Astra, 49.1% to 42.8% on FrontierCode 2.0 and 69.9% to 65.5% on FrontierSWE v2. Fable’s 49.1% came at X high effort. At High, its default on the Claude API, it scored 45.3%. Benchmark leads don’t always carry over to real work.

The cost side is less simple than the price list. Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and AI companies bill by them. At standard API rates, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra in September at standard API rates of $10 per million uncached input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. “The price per task is what matters,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said at Astra’s launch. Both APIs charge for reasoning tokens as output and have separate rates for cached input.

In my experience, Anthropic’s models have used more tokens than OpenAI’s. I put this positioning to the test and ran Fable 5.2 against Astra on tasks that simulate real developer work.

The tests

I ran both models on the same three tasks, once each, through each vendor’s API at default settings. Each test is worth 50 points, and I used a script to grade all the answers. Here are the tests:

Bug fix: I planted 10 bugs in a 2,600-line billing codebase and wrote a support ticket describing 10 customer complaints. The ticket’s guesses about the causes are wrong, two of the codebase’s own tests are wrong, and one bug only shows up after another is fixed.

Code review: I planted 45 defects in its VAT ID checks for 27 countries, its IBAN rules, its European Central Bank payment calendar, and its date formats for 50 locales in an EU invoicing package. The models had to prove each defect with an input the code gets wrong and identify the correct answer. Flagging false alarms cost the models points.

Code writing: The model wrote the same helpers from scratch, including VAT ID validation for 27 countries, IBAN checks for 34 countries, the payment calendar, and long dates.

Bug fix

Fable 5.2 and Astra fixed all 10 bugs and passed all 50 hidden checks, both in 12 turns (the matching number of turns surprised me).

The difference is in how much each model spent to get there. Fable 5.2 used more than 17,000 reasoning tokens, and Astra used 819 (wow). Astra passed the checks in about two minutes at an estimated cost of 98 cents. Fable 5.2 took more than five minutes and cost an estimated $2.51.

The numbers:

Fable 5.2: 12 turns, 696,863 in, 36,135 out (17,387 reasoning), $2.51, 326 s.

Astra: 12 turns, 231,854 in, 6,823 out (819 reasoning), $0.98, 122 s.

Code review

This is the only test where the scores differ. Fable 5.2 scored 49, and Astra scored 45. Fable 5.2 proved 44 of the 45 defects and raised no false alarms across 71 findings. Astra proved 41 and incorrectly classified one Spanish ID as valid. Astra missed defects in check-digit rules for Spain, Ireland, and Luxembourg. Both models missed the same Spanish defect: two swapped letters in a 23-letter lookup table.

Fable 5.2’s thoroughness came at a price. It cost more than six times what Astra did and took more than four times as long. If your code handles invoices (or simple approvals), one validation rule the review misses can get real invoices rejected, so Fable 5.2’s four extra points may be worth the higher price. For a routine review, Astra found 91% of the defects for 16% of the cost. Each model ran once, so a four-point gap could shift on another run.

The numbers:

Fable 5.2: 26 turns, 2,207,564 in, 103,240 out (77,641 reasoning), $6.05, 993 s.

Astra: 12 turns, 192,018 in, 8,664 out (4,307 reasoning), $0.95, 227 s.

Code writing

Both models scored 50 of 50. Each one wrote working checks for 27 countries’ VAT IDs and 34 countries’ IBANs with no libraries to lean on. Neither model had trouble here. Both passed all the checks in one run.

Astra took 23 turns, almost as many as Fable 5.2’s 24. Fable 5.2 still cost 2.3 times as much and took 1.7 times as long for the same score. In this run, the extra tokens didn’t raise the score.

The numbers:

Fable 5.2: 24 turns, 1,495,712 in, 87,542 out (47,458 reasoning), $4.83, 838 s.

Astra: 23 turns, 460,271 in, 24,007 out (9,328 reasoning), $2.06, 483 s.

Results

Test Claude Fable 5.2 GPT-6 Astra

Bug fix (of 50) 50 50

Code review (of 50) 49 45

Code writing (out of 50) 50 50

Total tokens in / out 4,400,139 / 226,917 884,143 / 39,494

Estimated cost $13.39 $3.99

Total time 2,157 s 832 s

Fable 5.2 led on code review and tied Astra on the other two tasks. Across the two tied tasks, its estimated API cost was 2.4 times Astra’s ($7.34 vs. $3.04), and it took 1.9 times as long (1,164 vs. 605 seconds).

What do I think?

For tasks like these, I’d start with Astra. It matched Fable 5.2’s scores on bug fixing and code writing at about 41% of the estimated cost, and it finished all three tasks faster. I’d consider Fable 5.2 for a careful code review, where it found three more defects in this test. Both models missed defects.

Fable 5.2’s standard token rates are lower, but it used about five times as many tokens as Astra across these three runs. Brockman’s point about price per task held up here.

articles.title: Weeks after shipment was swiped by China, Pentagon ‘struggles to account for’ $31 billion in missing F-35 aircraft parts
articles.description: The Pentagon is struggling to track an astonishing 26 million F-35 warfighter parts, worth an estimated $31 billion, according to analysis published by the Government Accountability Office this week.
articles.content:
The Pentagon is struggling to track an astonishing 26 million F-35 warfighter parts, worth an estimated $31 billion, according to analysis published by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) this week. In its report — published just weeks after China purportedly swiped a classified shipment of F-35 parts diverted through Hong Kong — the GAO criticized the current inventory system as “outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete.” Possible solutions were also provided by the GAO; however, the implications are that the most advanced and costly fighter jets in U.S. history may not be ready and reliable due to inventory management deficiencies.

Inventory problems have been a long-standing feature of the deployment of the F-35, notes the source. The F-35 program is estimated to cost $1.9 trillion over its lifecycle. It is the most costly weapon system in history, says the GAO. But the Department of Defense (DOD) has “long-standing and ongoing deficiencies related to the accountability and financial reporting of F-35 parts,” asserts the watchdog.

Chief among the issues that need to be addressed is the headlining massive unmonitored pool of roughly 26 million spare parts. These are spread among 700 government and contractor facilities worldwide, but the technology for managing massive inventories has existed for decades.

We might have seen a telling symptom of the inadequate F-35 parts tracking system back in September. A communications and/or accountability breakdown resulted in a UPS worker routing top-secret parts through Hong Kong to save time. They were allegedly swiped by China after an employee is thought to have missed an email warning not to divert the parts.

“Minimal progress” since 2019

Frustratingly, this is the third report since 2019 from the GAO, and the latest published report complains that the DOD has “made minimal progress” in implementing past recommendations. For example, in a 2022 report, periodic physical inventories of F-35 parts were recommended but have not been implemented yet, notes Stars and Stripes. There is also no reliable procedure for verifying data from prime contractors, which can be “inaccurate and incomplete.”

Currently, it is believed that there are over 1 million parts, worth more than $85 million, that are lost or missing. Moreover, about 17,000 parts that have been sent in for repair, worth as much as $42.5 billion, aren’t tracked.

“Live connection” inventory system

Stars and Stripes mentions that the Pentagon is working on “a live connection” for the F-35 Joint Program Office (JPO), bridging its inventory software and that of prime contractors with F-35 parts. The JPO asserts that it is now modernizing its infrastructure with direct real-time interfaces. “This integration directly addresses previous system gaps to ensure seamless accountability of F-35 spare parts,” said a JPO spokesperson, quoted by Breaking Defense.

articles.title: Lawyer’s eight-V100 AI server moves DeepSeek from 2-bit to near-NVFP4 precision
articles.description: A lawyer’s eight-GPU Nvidia V100 server now runs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash’s most-used experts at NVFP4 precision instead of 2-bit.
articles.content:
A lawyer with a private AI server built on eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs returned with an update, moving about 80% of its work up from 2-bit to 4-bit NVFP4 precision and bringing in 1TB of RAM and an RTX 3090. The server uses DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with a legal harness, the workflows and checks he wraps around the model, for his law practice. The cost? Performance, with code output dropping from 160–215 to 150–180 tokens per second, although the crashes that hit the new build are gone. The culprit behind the crashes, originally blamed on PCIe, was likely a bad PSU.

Lawyer's V100 homelab, update 2: the 8x V100 box now runs DeepSeek at near-NVFP4 precision with a 524K context, a 3090 moved in, RAM went to 1 TB, and I blamed PCIe for what was probably one bad PSU  from  r/homelab

Once a random hardware nerd lawyer on Reddit, the lawyer's responses to the original breaking story illuminated his identity. He’s a trial lawyer in Columbia, South Carolina. ProprietaryLegalAI commented on our first story three times, linking to a code repository, site, and LinkedIn that identify him as Nick Mermiges, founder of PLI Labs and proprietarylegal.ai. His other firm, PLI, is a technology consultancy, not a law firm, and now lists private, on-prem LLM serving as a service.

He built the software side with AI, specifically Claude Code, which wrote the kernels and ran the benchmarks with his direction. The Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 models handled the optimizations, custom kernels, and re-quantizing; he noted he was surprised at how well Fable built custom Volta kernels, and how it re-quantizes the experts his legal harness triggers. From about February to July, he built a legal harness around Claude that worked, while his attempts at a local-model version failed, but then DeepSeek V4.1 Flash arrived, and he was able to port it successfully, even if he says it’s not as good as frontier.

He reaffirms that “the documents never leave the office” and upgraded the system from 256GB to 1TB of RAM and tossed in a newer GPU, even as the V100s stay on “borrowed time” with R580, the last Nvidia driver branch to support them. The project’s intentions, as listed last time, suggested he wanted the system to be able to offload more of his workload, so this and the precision change are a reasonable upgrade. His previously stated goal of wanting the system to handle more than one request at a time has also been met.

The original “Volta sPLIt” build we covered has transformed into the “Volta Max uPLIft,” still with the clever lettering as his company’s initials are PLI — Proprietary Legal Intelligence. He now claims “near-NVFP4 precision,” having described NVFP4 on our forum earlier this week as “essentially full precision.” NVFP4 is Nvidia’s 4-bit floating-point format, and Nvidia publishes its own NVFP4 version of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; the project’s README says that version matches the precision of the model’s official weights at 4.25 bits per weight.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is built from “experts,” the parts of the model that do most of the work for each word. This model didn’t fit at that precision before, as 384 routed experts, in each of 40 layers, counts to 15,360 in all. At official precision, this comes out to about 269 GiB, by his estimate, and eight 32GB V100s have 256 GiB in total before anything else is loaded. With the 2-bit build, the weights were 248.8GB; the new build’s Hugging Face package is about 556GB.

The workaround is to keep every expert on the cards at 2-bit and swap the most-used ones up until the cards are full, which in this case came out to about 38.7%, or 5,949 experts, at precisely NVFP4. “Most-used,” in this context, refers to a count from a mix of four kinds of text, which are weighted equally, one of which is his own legal harness traffic.

The payoff is that those experts do most of the work. In testing with one request at a time, between 80% and 86% of decode routes, the calls to an expert made while the model writes, land on the NVFP4 experts, lowest for general text and highest for source code. The prediction for the two-request setup he runs is 78% to 85%. The remaining 15% to 22% of calls would still go to a 2-bit expert.

Measured against Nvidia’s own version of the model as the reference, he was able to get good results. Same next token, or how often a build picks the same next token as the reference, went up to 95.1% from 92.2%. For KL divergence, which measures how far a build’s probabilities are from the reference’s, it went down to 0.079 nats from 0.196. In measuring multiple-choice answers that change, across 513 questions from a standard multiple-choice knowledge test, it went from 79 different to just 8.

This does not measure accuracy — which was about the same across all three cases — but fidelity. Those tests ran on the build’s first release, but not on the new two-request setup he now runs.

The result of the changes: higher fidelity but at a lower level of performance. Code output is 3% to 30% slower, depending on the prompt length, and legal writing is 9% to 23% slower. Before the build, he hoped to maintain about 80 tokens per second on legal and prose; the bench came in at 86 to 106 for legal and 78 to 86 for prose. The upside is that running two requests at once raises total output to 159.0 tokens per second, versus 118.9 with a sole request. The first token also arrives sooner at every prompt length, 108.4 seconds versus 118.7 seconds at 256K tokens.

Each request needs a “slot,” though, and this comes at a cost. Every slot keeps its own state on the cards, which leaves room for fewer NVFP4 experts: 6,215, 5,949, 5,663 for one, two, and three slots, respectively. This means each added slot may push another one to two points of the calls back to 2-bit, which could reduce output quality.

The move to more RAM came this week with eight 128GB modules at 2,933 MT/s, originally eight 32GB modules that had to be run at DDR4-2666 due to ECC errors. After the RAM upgrade, the host reports two NUMA nodes, and two boots hung at the first transfer between the boards, so he reordered the cards in software. The GPUs remain capped at 1,522 MHz, as before.

As for the PSU, he took the common approach of chasing PCIe slots, cards, and cables to narrow down the cause, finally concluding it was “probably one bad PSU.” He also added more fans, but with no temperature changes, this only indicated that airflow was not the problem. He changed the power delivery, and nine of nine long chats read clean afterward. Also, don’t judge his cable management skill; any “advice [there] is welcome and will be ignored,” which is the only comment to make in that situation.

He also already has two DGX Sparks running the same model at 1M context for agent work, and three or four sessions at once, and he isn’t stopping there. Now it comes down to scaling. Eight more V100s and a second server, with 512GB of 3,200 MT/s ECC RAM, are waiting in the wings. The second box would run another high-precision DeepSeek, used as an extra agent or to run tasks in parallel. The plan is also to move DeepSeek’s small draft model off the V100s and onto the RTX 3090, which hasn’t happened yet.

articles.title: China’s Air Force builds drone that shoots painkiller darts at wounded soldiers
articles.description: The Air Force Medical University of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) built this drone so it could remotely administer pain killers to injured soldiers and make extraction easier.
articles.content:
A Chinese military medical school has just developed a UAV that could remotely administer medicine, helping treat injured soldiers on the front lines without putting medical personnel at risk. According to Chinese mouthpiece Global Times, the Air Force Medical University built the first casualty-search drone for the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) that fires darts loaded with painkillers to help ease the pain of wounded personnel.

“We have developed the military’s first casualty-search drone and have also made some breakthroughs in treatment. For example, we can use drones to inject medication into wounded personnel from a considerable distance,” Air Force Medical University representative Wang Jianqi told the publication. “Wherever our drone can fly, we can deliver life-saving emergency medication into a wounded person’s muscle, buying valuable time for treatment.”

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine saw the widespread use of drones on the frontline, primarily for search-and-destroy and reconnaissance missions. However, the four-year escalation of the 12-year war has seen the creative implementations of these units — from jam-proof fiber optic drones to the use of heavy-lift hexacopters for medical evacuation. Now, drones-as-first-responders are being developed for civilian use, including firefighting drones, camera response drones, and even “Campus Guardian Angel” drones designed to neutralize school shooters.

However, China's air-ground treatment drone remains in the experimental stage, says Wang. After all, you can’t just administer medication without assessing the patient’s vital signs and their injuries. It’s also difficult or even impossible to load an incapacitated soldier without external assistance. Still, the deployment of medical UAVs would help with battlefield medicine, which has developed the concept of the “golden hour,” which suggests that wounded personnel treated within the first hour have the greatest chance of survival.

Although battlefield medicine was in use since the 1800s, especially during Napoleon’s invasion of Russia and the American Civil War, helicopter medevacs were first deployed during World War 2 in Burma and the Philippines. The Korean War saw the introduction of MASH — Mobile Army Surgical Hospital — units that brought forward treatment units closer to the frontline.

This, combined with the widespread use of UH-1 Hueys during the Vietnam War to evacuate wounded soldiers from the front lines, sometimes while under enemy fire, has greatly increased the survival rate among wounded soldiers. Today, helicopter and ground medevacs are common among military forces, with drone treatment and evacuation now being experimented with in both the frontlines of Ukraine and military medical universities in China.

articles.title: Commemorative plaque at Denny’s booth where Nvidia was born has been removed in wake of Jensen Huang scandals
articles.description: The San Jose, California, branch of Denny's once featured a plaque commemorating the booth where Jensen Huang and his two other co-founders worked to build Nvidia.
articles.content:
Jensen Huang was one of the American success stories in Silicon Valley, where he had his humble beginnings as a seasonal dishwasher, busboy, and waiter at his nearby Denny’s before he rose to stardom as the head of Nvidia. The diner honored this achievement with a plaque at the booth where Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem met after their working hours and first planned the inception of Nvidia. However, NBC News said that the sign has since been removed following Huang’s spectacular fall from grace and resignation from the company.

Unfortunately, employees say that the commemorative plaque, which read, “The booth that launched a $1 trillion company,” has been removed. It remains unclear who ordered the removal, though, so we reached out to Denny’s for comment and will update the story if they answer.

Despite being a billionaire, the former Nvidia CEO is known for keeping in touch with his roots. He has been spotted several times eating street food and enjoying local fast food in the various cities that he visits. He even once dragged the 35 Taiwanese industry chiefs to a restaurant in Taipei, earning that event the moniker “ trillion-dollar banquet.” This “man of the people” persona has made him quite a popular figure among some people, fueling the Jensanity hype, especially in his home country of Taiwan.

We also saw this side of Jensen during the unveiling of the plaque in 2023, after Nvidia hit a $1 trillion valuation, when he balanced 10 plates and served food during the event. The restaurant also put up a food truck and served “Nvidia Breakfast Bytes” at GTC 2025, which consisted of four sausage links served with four buttermilk silver dollar pancakes and some syrup, and was available for a limited time for under $5 in all Denny’s branches across the country.

This move is just another sign of Jensen’s sudden downfall. He was still the leader of one of the most valuable companies in the world a couple of weeks ago, evangelizing artificial intelligence to anyone willing to listen. Today finds a totally different reality, with sources saying that he looked “broken and shattered,” and he even called himself “a piece of sh--” as he left the company he built for over 30 years after the board ousted him.

There is no telling yet what’s next for Jensen Huang. Elon Musk has reportedly offered him a position, saying that it “would be an honor” to hire the person who was arguably one of the biggest driving forces in today’s AI industry, but he’s also facing numerous investigations from both his company, Congress, and the FBI. More importantly, Jensen will have to deal with the fallout of the revelations on his public image and personal life.

articles.title: Mechatronics student builds 3D printer made from 92% LEGO for less than $180
articles.description: A mechatronics engineering student made an open-source 3D printer, 92% of which is LEGO, and can print a decent benchy despite the imprecise LEGO leadscrews.
articles.content:
Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO. The bill of materials only totals $173.35, with $30 of the budget going to LEGO pieces that comprise 92% of the whole build. Turaj’s project got him flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, where he got to meet Prusa CMO Zack Freedman and presented Studprint to over 4,000 people at the event.

Earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers. Whoever submits a benchy with their printer gets a chance to be flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, and Turaj was one of them.

Turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS. He named the project Studprint, referring to the studs on a LEGO brick. What takes this project even farther is that Turaj decided he would only use “classical LEGO,” avoiding LEGO Technic pieces wherever possible. Looking at the repository’s images of the CAD designs, you would easily mistake it for a virtual LEGO builder.

Turaj shared an image of the bill of materials (BOM) on the GitHub repository for his build, showing a final build price of $173.35. There are three major electronics components in the printer: the first is the BTT SKR Pico V1.0, a control board commonly used in open-source 3D printers like the Voron V0; for wireless capability, a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is used; and the whole printer is powered by a Mean Well LRS-150-24 switching power supply — with all three components priced at around $25 each. This printer is built with the backbone of a true DIY 3D-printer build, unlike this cute LEGO 3D printer we covered last year that used a 3D printing pen.

There are five NEMA 17 stepper motors, also popular in 3D printers, whether open- or closed-source. Four of the motors control the axes, while the fifth is used to feed filament to the Trianglelab V6 Extruder. The rest of the 3D printer is made of $30 worth of LEGO pieces; even the build plate is a block of LEGO. Turaj’s only print shown on the GitHub repository is a Benchy, sliced in Klipper and printed in 1.25 hours; it’s surprisingly good considering the leadscrews are all LEGO pieces.

articles.title: Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
articles.description: Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services
articles.content:
The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.

As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like. Or, for that matter, other US tech giants.

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.

A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud."

A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't."

The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly."

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure. Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.

Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register: "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.

"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy."

Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®

articles.title: Breaking Down Theo's Shock Moment in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 and the Mystery of His Father With Actor Tyroe Muhafidin
articles.description: A spoiler-filled The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 interview with Theo actor Tyroe Muhafidin.
articles.content:
Warning! Spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Episodes 1-4 follow.

If you’re caught up with The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, you’ll have watched Season 3, Episode 4 and were probably left reeling by a shock character death that leaves the elves in a spot of bother going into the final stretch.

During the first four episodes of Season 3, we see Theo, played by Tyroe Muhafidin, tempted by Sauron into becoming a Nazgnagôl. Nazgnagôl are men who wear one of Sauron’s Rings of Power, but still retain something of their humanity. That is, they are not fully Nazgûl, or Ringwraiths, as we know of the beings in the Third Age of J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth. They are, at this stage, Ring Servants.

Theo, last seen as a hopeful child of the Southlands and friend of hero elf Arondir, is now older and full of hate after five years of Númenórean oppression. Sauron sees something in him, something special, and offers Theo a gift. In Episode 2, appropriately called The Gift of Men, Sauron performs a dark ritual that lets Theo “meet” his mysterious father, or at least that’s what we think is happening here (with Sauron, you never really know!).

This is a callback to a scene in Season 1 where a young Theo encounters The Hilt, a broken sword-hilt forged during the First Age. It had been left hidden in a barn where Theo discovers it, and we see Theo’s blood drip into the Hilt, somehow feeding its regeneration. Clearly, Theo had some dark power inside him, although it was left unaddressed, sparking many fan theories over recent years.

In Season 3, Sauron notices the dark mark left on Theo’s arm after his interaction with The Hilt and immediately raises an eyebrow. Who was Theo’s father, really? During the ritual, Sauron uses the power of necromancy to communicate with the dead in the Unseen World. Sauron listens to the words of the dead, and tells Theo his father was named Fäldred, Son of Hammethreg. Theo asks, “Who are you, father?” The response, in Black Speech, is “Gorthmundur.” Sauron tells Theo this was a “Noble House of old, the sworn stewards of Mordor blessed with… certain powers.”

These powers, it seems, were passed down to Theo. “There is a reason you were drawn to that hilt, and it to you,” Sauron continues, before suggesting that Theo might have become ruler of the Southlands had his mother not “hidden the truth.” Theo responds to say his mother told him his father left. Sauron disputes this, before issuing a revelation that sends Theo spiralling: his mother murdered his father over what he had become.

Sauron, ever the opportunist, offers Theo a Ring of Power. He tells him that he has the power within him to become “a conqueror, a sorcerer, a king.” The downcast Theo accepts the gift.

Fast forward to Episode 4, and one of two shock deaths that punctuate this first block of The Rings of Power Season 3. Theo, now in full Nazgnagôl gear and spurred on by Sauron, murders his friend Arondir during the escape from Gundabad. It’s a shocking twist that cements Theo’s descent into darkness, and marks the end of the road for one of the mighty heroes of The Rings of Power.

In the interview below, I ask Tyroe Muhafidin about Theo’s journey in these first four episodes, what it’s like to play a Nazgnagôl, and where the murder of Arondir leaves The Rings of Power. And yes, we get into the question of Theo’s parentage. Was Sauron telling him the truth about his father?

IGN: The first question is an obvious one: how does it feel to be playing a Nazgnagôl?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It was crazy. The costume automatically gives you a sense of such great strength and power. The biggest thing for me was, as soon as I put on those gauntlets there was an automatic transforming moment for me where you could just feel the power through your body. And it's interesting because I went from playing basically a helpless child to some godlike being. So it was a real jump and I had to do a lot of work in terms of my physicality and trying to look powerful and strong, which was something so new to me because I've always been scrawny and helpless. So yeah, it was a challenge, but I think I got there in the end, and I'm super, super grateful that I've got a chance to be something so iconic and to play something so iconic.

IGN: What is your understanding of what Nazgnagôl are, as it was explained to you?

Tyroe Muhafidin: So a Nazgûl directly translates to Ringwraith, whereas Nazgnagôl directly translates to Ring Servant. At this point in time when we've just put the ring on, we're not quite wraiths yet. We are still human men with autonomy over their body and can make their own decisions. We're just a lot stronger now. We've got a lot of power and a lot of dark power.

An important thing to know is at the beginning of this season, the One Ring hasn't yet been made. So these rings are yet to be binded completely to Sauron's will, where we are not now complete, I guess, his minions. We still have autonomy over who we are. That was the fun thing to play in this season, the gradual descent into more and more madness and more and more evil and darkness. But at this point in time, we get to very much still be people, just very strong people, I guess.

IGN: There's a really interesting scene where Sauron reveals Theo's parentage to him. What's your understanding of who Theo's father is? Sauron is suggesting at that moment that Theo has an innate power as a result of his parentage, but it's left ambiguous. And Sauron looks emotional even as he's talking to Theo about this. I almost was thinking he almost looks at him as his own son in some ways. So what's your read on that? What can you tell us about what all that means?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It's revealed that his father was the head of a few dark sorcerers and he sided with the dark side a long time ago, alongside his peers and the other Southlanders who sided with Sauron. And so there's that kind of information that's brought out.

But I think the big thing for Theo is when Sauron says his mother killed him when she found out. And I think that moment for me, and I think for Theo as a whole, it kind of sends a spin in the works of, what is Sauron really doing here and what is he trying to accomplish? Is he just trying to say words to make Theo happy, trying to build this broken boy up? Because he can see something for sure. And I don't think Theo really realizes. But I think there was always a dark side to Theo and maybe it was inherited, but that relationship to the Hilt was always something that stuck with him.

And I think maybe when he got a taste of that darkness in the Hilt, maybe it was the first time he kind of felt the presence of his father, and maybe that's why it was so addictive, that feeling to him. So I think this season we find out a little bit more of where he comes from.

But I think the biggest thing is, how much of it is the truth? What is Sauron saying that is manipulation and deceit and what is the truth? Which I think is kind of the fun dynamic of those scenes, is you feel like you're finding out a lot, but are you really?

IGN: There is a big moment in Episode 4 where Theo kills Arondir, a character who's been in the series from the beginning. When you first found out you'd be doing that, what was your reaction?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It was interesting. I was excited because I was like, "Oh, this is some juicy stuff to get into." But I think the moment I got the script, I found out and I was really excited because it was going to be some really cool stuff. When I read it all, it all became very real for me. And it was like, "Wow, this is a big task. This is super daunting." And there were months of intense anxiety coming up to this moment. But yeah, I guess I was just super excited, but anxious at the same time. And I feel like I knew at some point something big like this was going to happen. So I think it was just a matter of being prepared for it and trying to service Ismail [Cruz Córdova, who plays Arondir] as well, the best I possibly could.

IGN: What do you think the character death means for the show at that point and the story it's telling, but also for Theo? Do you see it as this is a moment that we see a tipping point in him that the audience is like, "Okay, yes, he has really gone too far."

Tyroe Muhafidin: In terms of the show, it's a moment of no-one is safe and there's no mercy from the dark side. And this war is very much real. The most talented and bravest of your warriors will go down. And that's kind of, I think, setting the premise for the rest of the war that's going to go on.

I think for Theo specifically, it definitely was that tipping point where his decision is made and his destiny is decided. And I think he realizes this afterwards as well, and whether he agrees with that decision he's made or not, he's made that decision.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 episodes 1-4 are out now on Prime Video. Check back with IGN after Episodes 5 and 6 are released this week for more.

articles.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
articles.description: Accessing banned content is as easy as whipping out a thesaurus, Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee hears
articles.content:
Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.

A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters.

Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms.

"Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said.

"I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable.

"So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently."

McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not.

"If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added.

"And we know your algorithm would."

Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too.

Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal.

She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly.

There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs.

"So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content."

Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories.

With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process.

Success of user reports trails away

As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially.

Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent.

Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures.

The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly.

Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests.

Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report, it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny.

Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment.

The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force.

England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference " to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves.

Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms.

She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.'

"In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered.

"So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

articles.title: James Gunn Shuts Down Rumors That Skydance Is Meddling With Man of Tomorrow
articles.description: James Gunn has shut down rumors that the new DC overseers at Skydance have meddled with his cut of Man of Tomorrow following his shocking DC Studios exit.
articles.content:
James Gunn has shut down rumors that the new DC overseers at Skydance have meddled with his cut of Man of Tomorrow following his shocking DC Studios exit.

The internet has filled with gossip in the wake of Gunn and Peter Safran's departure as co-chairmen of the comic book entertainment wing earlier this week. As an ocean of rumors rises, some of the more worrying claims have seen some suggest Skydance has already taken control of the Superman director's sequel, which could result in major characters like Supergirl and Blue Beetle being cut entirely.

These are just some of the accusations that Gunn sought to dispel in a Threads post tonight. In what is essentially his first public statement since leaving DC Studios, the filmmaker took aim at the gossip that has DCU fans concerned. Not only have "sweeping changes" to Man of Tomorrow not been made, but apparently, no one at Skydance has even seen his movie yet.

"There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen Man of Tomorrow and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made," he said. "No one from Skydance has even seen the movie - the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false."

It's a response that will not answer every question comic book movie enjoyers have about the future of the DCU, but it does clear the air about much of the more damning chatter online. Gunn's comments mean that any talk of Skydance being unhappy with the current cut of Man of Tomorrow is false. It also sounds like, at least for now, Supergirl and Blue Beetle, who had been previously reported to return, are safe.

With so much time left before David Corenswet's Clark Kent returns to theaters in July, though, it's hard to say how the Skydance takeover may impact its release. It's best to wait until Gunn or Skydance has more to share before setting any firm expectations in place for now.

All of that said, it's not too hard to see why fans of the DCU have felt uneasy in the last few days. Gunn and Safran have orchestrated the DCU to tell a varied collection of superpowered stories for four years, with its overarching plan for the years ahead only just starting to come into view. Pulling them from the driver's seat means the future is more unknown than ever before, especially considering Skydance was quick to find a replacement in Marvel alum Jeremy Latcham.

Will Man of Tomorrow be altered against Gunn's will? Will Skydance reboot the DC movie universe and scrap future plans for the DCU? How will any of this affect future entries in Robert Pattinson's The Batman saga? It's all too soon to tell, but that won't stop the rumor mill from pushing ahead.

What we do know is what Gunn shared with fans in the immediate aftermath of his exit. In a letter posted to social media, he promised that the characters he and Safran helped set up "will live on." He also confirmed that the duo was recently "engaged on another DC project" that he is writing. What that project is remains a mystery.

For more on the future of the DCU, you can read up on what we know about Latcham. You can also check out another report that suggested Skydance intends to prioritize more well-known heroes in the DC portfolio going forward. Man of Tomorrow, meanwhile, is set to premiere July 9, 2027.
